Mujahid said: ﴿and they tilled the land﴾ means they ploughed it. Al-Farra' said: they turned it over for cultivation. Others said: they turned the surface of the earth over to extract water, to extract minerals, and to cast seed into it for cultivation. And "ithara" (tilling) is moving a thing until its dust rises. Abu Ja'far read: "wa-ātharū al-arḍa," with a long vowel after the hamza. Ibn Mujahid said: That is nothing, and Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) explained it as lengthening of the vowel, like the line:

"And whoever blames time for one who has departed,"

and he said: it is due to poetic necessity and does not occur in the Qur'an. Al-Hasan (?) — rather, Abu Haywa read: "wa-āthirū," from al-atharah, which is monopolizing a thing. It was also read: "wa-athrū al-arḍa," meaning: they left traces of themselves upon it.

﴿And they built it﴾ from ʿimārah (cultivation/building), meaning: their staying in it was longer than the staying of these people; or from ʿumrān (settlement), meaning: they dwelt in it; or from ʿimārah. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿more than they built it﴾ refers to the building of the people of Makkah, and the people of Makkah are people of a valley without cultivation; they have no tilling of the land at all, nor any building whatsoever. So this is nothing but mockery of them and belittling of their state in their world, because most of what the people of the world rely upon and boast of is the matter of wealthy landowners (dahqana), and they too are weak in strength. ﴿So Allah would not have wronged them﴾: before it there is something omitted, meaning: they denied them, so they were destroyed. The two Ḥaramayn (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and Abu 'Amr read: "thumma kāna ʿāqibatu" with the nominative, as the subject of "kāna," and its predicate is "al-sūʾā," or it is the feminine of al-asʾa (the worst), from al-sūʾ (evil).

﴿That they denied﴾ is an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlihi) connected to the predicate, not to "asāʾa," for otherwise there would be a separation between the relative clause and its complement by the predicate, and that is not permitted. The meaning: then their end was, so the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun. ﴿The worst (al-sūʾā)﴾ means: the punishment which is the worst of punishments in the Hereafter, and it is Hell. It is also permissible that "al-sūʾā" be a verbal noun on the pattern fu'lā, like "al-ruj'ā," and be a predicate too. It is also permissible that it be an object of "asāʾa" in the sense of "they committed," and an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: the evil worst; and the predicate of "kāna" would be "an kadhdhabū." Al-A'mash and al-Hasan read: "al-sūwā," replacing the hamza with a waw and assimilating the waw into it, like the reading of the one who read "bi-l-sūwwi" with assimilation in (Surah) Yusuf. Ibn Mas'ud read: "al-sū'a," with masculine gender. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read: "ʿāqibata" with the accusative, as predicate of "kāna," and the noun is "al-sūʾā," or "al-sūʾa" as object, and "kadhdhabū" is the noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that "an" be in the sense of "ay" (that is): the explanation of the evil is the denial and mockery, and "kāna" is in the sense of "qāla," as in "nādā" and "kataba." Another possibility is that ﴿they committed the evil (asāʾū al-sūʾā)﴾ means: they committed the sin which is the worst of sins, and ﴿that they denied﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to it, and the predicate of "kāna" is omitted, as the answer of "lammā" and "law" is omitted for the purpose of vagueness. End of quotation. That "an" here is a particle of explanation (ḥarf tafsīr) is very forced. As for his phrase "al-khaṭāyāt" (the sins), it is so in the copy we consulted, pluralized with the broken plural with alif and ta', and that is not a regular pattern; it is only restricted to what is heard. It is not far that the addition of the ta' in "al-khaṭāyāt" comes from the copyist. As for his statement: "and ﴿that they denied﴾ is an explicative apposition to it, that is, to the worst, and the predicate of 'kāna' is omitted, etc." — this is a non-Arab understanding, because the sentence is independent and very good without omission, so one would have to invent an omitted element indicated by a sign. Our companions (the grammarians of our school) do not permit omitting the predicate of "kāna" and its sisters, either as a shortening or an abbreviation, except where something of it has been transmitted, and then it is not used as a general rule.

Abdullah and Talha read: "yubdi'u" with a dammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the dāl; the majority read it with a fatḥah. The two Abus (Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far?) read: "yurja'ūna" with the third-person yā'; the majority with the second-person tā', meaning: to His reward and His punishment. The majority read: ﴿yublisu﴾ with a kasrah on the lām; ʿAlī and al-Sulami read it with a fatḥah, from "abalsahu," when he silenced him. The majority read: "wa-lam yakun" with yā'; Kharija and al-Aris, both from Nafi', and Ibn Sinan from Abu Ja'far, and al-Antaki from Shayba, read with the feminine tā'.

﴿From their associates﴾ means: from those whom they worshipped besides Allah, and they are the idols, and they were attributed to them because they associated them in their wealth. It was said: because they took them, in their assumption, as partners of Allah. Muqatil said: the intended are the angels, intercessors with Allah, as they claimed: ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ (Al-Zumar: 3). ﴿And they will be﴾: its meaning is: and at their witnessing the command of Allah and the corruption of the state of the idols, He expressed it in the past tense to affirm the matter and the soundness of its occurrence. ﴿Al-sūʾā﴾ was written with an alif before the yā', as they wrote "ʿulamā'a Banī Isrā'īl" with a waw before the alif. The tanwin in ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is the tanwin of compensation for an omitted clause, meaning: ﴿and on the day the Hour is established﴾, the day when ﴿the criminals will be in despair﴾. The pronoun in ﴿they will be separated﴾ refers to the believers and the disbelievers, because of the indication of what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari said: It appears that it refers to what came before it, since before it is: ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾. Qatada said: it is a separation, with no reunion after it.

﴿In a garden (rawḍah)﴾: the rawḍah is land possessing plants and water. In the proverb: "more beautiful than an egg," meaning the eggs of the ostrich. The rawḍah is among the things that please the Arabs, and they have greatly praised it in their poetry.

﴿They will be made joyful (yuḥbarūn)﴾ means: they will be gladdened. Ḥabara-hu: he gladdened him with gladness, and his face brightened for him and its trace appeared upon him; yaḥburu with a ḍammah, ḥabran, ḥabratan, ḥubūran. In the proverb: "Their houses were filled with joy, so they await the tears." Al-Kisa'i related: "ḥabartuhu": I honored him and pampered him. ʿAlī ibn Sulayman said: it is from their saying: "there is a trace (ḥabrah) on his teeth," that is, a mark, meaning the trace of blessing flows over them. It was also said: from al-taḥbīr, which is beautification, meaning: they will be made beautiful. And it is said: "So-and-so has good ḥabr and sabr," with a fatḥah, when he is beautiful and of good appearance. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Mujahid said: they will be honored. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, al-Awza'i, and Waki' said: they will hear the songs. Abu Bakr and Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be crowned upon their heads. Ibn Kaysan said: they will be adorned. The meaning of ﴿brought forth (muḥḍarūn)﴾ is: gathered for it, none of them absent from it, by His saying: ﴿and they will not be out of it﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 37). The word "in a garden" came indefinite, and in the punishment definite. Al-Zamakhshari said: The indefiniteness is to suggest its unknown nature and magnify it. "Yuḥbarūn" came in the present verb form, because it is used for renewal, since every hour there comes to them what gladdens them of renewed delights of various kinds. "Muḥḍarūn" came in the active participle form, because it is used for permanence: so when they enter the punishment they remain in it as brought forth, and this is a necessary attribute of them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 30, verses 1–16 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 160] Surat al-Rum is Meccan.
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ ﴿in the nearest land. But after their defeat they will be victorious﴾ ﴿within a few years. The command belongs to God, before and after. On that day the believers will rejoice﴾ ﴿in God's victory. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿God's promise. God does not break His promise, but most people do not know﴾ ﴿They know the outward appearance of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves? God created the heavens and the earth and what is between them only with truth and for a specified term. Yet many people deny the meeting with their Lord﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen what was the end of those before them? They were stronger than them in power, and they ploughed the earth and cultivated it more than these have cultivated it. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. God would not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst evil: that they denied the signs of God and mocked them﴾ ﴿God originates creation, then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned﴾ ﴿On the day the Hour arises, the criminals will be dumbfounded﴾ ﴿They will have no intercessors from their associates, and they will disown their associates﴾ ﴿On the day the Hour arises, on that day they will be divided﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, they will be brought forth into the punishment﴾.

[p. 161] This surah is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyya and others said, without disagreement. Al-Zamakhshari said: except His saying: ﴿So glorified is God﴾ [al-Rum: 17].

Its occasion of revelation was that Kisra (the Persian king) sent an army against the Romans and appointed a man over them, and the narrators differed about his name. He marched against them with the people of Persia, prevailed, killed, destroyed, and cut down their olive trees. Their encounter took place at Adhri'at and Busra. Qaysar (the Byzantine emperor) had sent a man as commander over the Romans. Mujahid said: they met in al-Jazira. Al-Suddi said: in the land of Jordan and Palestine. This grieved the Muslims, because the Romans were People of the Book, and it pleased the polytheists, because the Persians (Majus) were not People of the Book. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) informed them that the Romans ﴿will be victorious within a few years﴾.

The first verses were revealed, and Abu Bakr proclaimed them in the outskirts of Mecca: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land. But after their defeat they will be victorious within a few years.﴾ Some of the polytheists of Quraysh said: Your companion claims that the Romans will defeat the Persians within a few years. Shall we wager on that with you? He said: Yes. This was before the prohibition of wagering (rihan). They agreed on a stake of a few years and three she-camels. Abu Bakr informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of this, and he said: "Why did you not make it bigger? Go back and increase them in the term and the wager." So they made the camels one hundred and the term nine years. The Romans prevailed over Persia in the seventh year. Among those who had wagered was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. When Abu Bakr wished to emigrate, Ubayy asked him for a guarantor for the wager in case the Romans won, and his son 'Abd al-Rahman guaranteed it. When Ubayy wished to go out to Uhud, 'Abd al-Rahman asked him for a guarantor, and he gave him one. Ubayy died from a wound that the Prophet (ﷺ) had inflicted on him. The Romans prevailed over Persia on the day of al-Hudaybiya. It was also said that the victory on the day of Badr was for both parties. Abu Bakr took the stake from the descendants of Ubayy and brought it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said to him: "Give it in charity."

The cause of the Romans' victory was that Kisra sent to Shahrayaz, who was the one he had appointed to fight the Romans, saying: "Kill your brother Farkhan for a statement he made, which was his saying: 'I saw myself sitting on the throne of Kisra.'" But he did not kill him. So Kisra sent to Persia that he had dismissed Shahrayaz and appointed his brother Farkhan, and wrote to him: when he takes office, he should kill his brother Shahrayaz. Farkhan intended to kill him, so Shahrayaz produced three letters from Kisra ordering him to kill his brother Farkhan. He said: "I have argued with you about your affair many times. Will you kill me on the strength of one letter?" So Farkhan returned the kingship to his brother. Shahrayaz wrote to Qaysar, the king of the Romans, and they cooperated against Kisra. The Romans defeated Persia, the news came, and the Muslims rejoiced. This was among the clear signs testifying to the authenticity of prophethood and that the Qur'an is from God, because it is a report of the unseen, which none knows except God.

Ali, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mu'awiya ibn Qurra and al-Hasan read ﴿ghulibat al-Rum﴾ with the verb active (ghalabat) and ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ with the verb passive (sayughlabun). The majority read ﴿ghulibat﴾ passive and ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ active. The interpretation of that, according to what Ibn 'Imran explained, is: the Romans were defeated in the nearest part of the countryside of Syria. By "rif" he means the cultivated land (al-sawad). This was also transmitted from Uthman. Abu Hatim interpreted it as: the Romans were defeated on the day of Badr, which was grievous to the disbelievers of Quraysh and pleased the believers, and God gave the good news to His servants that they would be victorious within a few years. End of quote. Thus he reports about the Romans that they have been defeated and that they will be victorious, so they were defeated twice. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reading with the ghayn vowelled with damma is more correct. People agreed on ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ with the ya vowelled with fatha, meaning the Romans. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he read "sayughlibun" with the ya vowelled with damma. In this reading the meaning transmitted by the reports is reversed. End of quote. His saying "they agreed" is not so. Do you not see that those who read "ghalabat" with fatha on the ghayn are the same ones who read "sayughlabun" with damma on the ya and fatha on the lam? And this reading is not specific to Ibn 'Umar. The majority read ﴿ghalabihim﴾ with fatha on the ghayn and the lam. Ali, Ibn 'Umar and Mu'awiya ibn Qurra read it with sukun. The analogous form from Ibn 'Umar would be "ghilabihim," on the pattern of "kitab."

[p. 162] The Rum: a group of Christians. "Adna al-ardh" means its nearest part. If the event took place at Adhri'at, then it is the nearest land in relation to Mecca, and this is what Imru' al-Qays mentioned in his saying:

I have looked upon it from Adhri'at, and its people are in Yathrib, the nearest of its dwellings with a high view.

If it was in al-Jazira, then it is nearest in relation to the land of Kisra. If it was in Jordan, then it is nearest in relation to the land of the Romans. Al-Kalbi read ﴿fi adna al-ardh﴾. The discussion of the meaning of "bid'" has already passed, in view of the two readings. So with "ghulibat," with damma on the ghayn, it is an idafa to the object; with fatha, it is an idafa to the subject, and the meaning is: the Muslims will defeat them within a few years, at the end of this period, which is the furthest extent of the meaning of "bid'."

The Muslims undertook jihad against the Romans. Our shaykh, the teacher Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, used to relate from Abu al-Hakam ibn Burjan that he derived from God's saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ up to His saying ﴿within a few years﴾ the conquest of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) by the Muslims, specifying its time and its day. At that time Jerusalem had come under Christian control. Ibn Burjan died before the time he had specified for the conquest, and after his death, after some time, the Muslims conquered it at the time Abu al-Hakam had specified. Abu Ja'far believed of this Abu al-Hakam that he would perceive some of the unseen matters, which he extracted from the Book of God.

﴿The command belongs to God﴾ means: the executing of rulings and their disposition as He wills. The majority read ﴿min qablu wa min ba'du﴾ with damma on both: that is, before the defeat of the Romans and after it. Since both are idafa to a definite noun and that noun is omitted, they are built on damma, and the discussion of this is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw). Abu al-Simmak, al-Jahdari and 'Awn al-'Uqayli read ﴿min qabl wa min ba'd﴾ with kasra and tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the genitive without assuming an omitted idafa, as if it were said: "qablan wa ba'dan," meaning "first and last." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: some Arabs say ﴿min qabl wa min ba'd﴾ with the genitive and tanwin. Al-Farra' said: it is also permissible to omit the tanwin, so that it remains as it is in idafa, even though the mudaf is omitted. End of quote. Al-Nahhas rejected what al-Farra' said, and said to al-Farra' in his book: there are many errors in the Qur'an in it, among them: he claimed that it is permissible to say "min qablu wa min ba'du," whereas it is only permissible to say "min qabl wa min ba'd" if they are indefinite, and the meaning is: from a previous one and from a later one. Al-Kisa'i reported from some of the Banu Asad: "lillahi al-amru min qablin wa min ba'du," the first genitive with tanwin, and the second with damma without tanwin.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is an adverbial complement of time for ﴿yafrahu al-mu'minun﴾ (the believers will rejoice), and on this meaning the exegetes explained it. It was also said: ﴿wa yawma'idhin﴾ is conjoined to ﴿min qablu wa min ba'du﴾, as if He had encompassed the three tenses: the past, the future and the present, and then began to report the rejoicing of the believers at the victory. And ﴿bi-nasr Allah﴾, that is, the Romans over Persia, or the Muslims over their enemy, or in the truth of what the Messenger (ﷺ) said, that the Romans will defeat Persia, or in that God empowers some of the wrongdoers over others until they destroy one another and turn away. These are possibilities. In a hadith: "Persia is a single blow or two blows, and there will be no Persia after them forever. The Romans are the people of horns; whenever one horn passes, another horn follows, until the end of time."

Ibn 'Abbas said: on the day of Badr was the defeat of the worshippers of idols and the worshippers of fire. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said the same. It was also said: news arrived on the day of al-Hudaybiya of the death of Kisra, and the Muslims rejoiced at the fighting of the polytheists and at the death of an enemy firmly established in the land. He is ﴿the Mighty﴾ in His vengeance upon His enemies, ﴿the Merciful﴾ to His friends. ﴿God's promise﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the previous sentence, which is His saying ﴿they will be victorious﴾ and His saying ﴿the believers will rejoice﴾.

﴿But most people﴾, the disbelievers of Quraysh and others, ﴿do not know﴾. He denied them knowledge that benefits for the Hereafter, while He affirmed for them knowledge of the affairs of this world. It was said: the meaning is that they do not know that affairs are from God, that His promise is not broken, and that what His Messenger (ﷺ) brings is true.

﴿They know the outward appearance﴾, that is, the manifest, which is what their senses perceive. It is as if their knowledge is merely the knowledge of animals. [p. 163] Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and the majority said: its meaning is what has manifestness and elevation in this world, such as the mastery of crafts and buildings, the places of earning wealth, agriculture, and the like. A group said: its meaning is what is passing and transient, that is, they know the affairs of this world, which has no permanence and no ultimate end. The poet al-Hudhali said:

The slanderers reproached her, saying I love her, and that is a complaint whose shame is manifestly removed from you.

That is, transient. Ibn Jubayr said: ﴿outward﴾ means they know it from the soothsayers, from what the devils steal. Al-Rummani said: whatever is known by the first sight is the outward, and whatever is known by the proof of reason is the inward. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they know﴾ is a substitute for ﴿they do not know﴾. In this substitution there is a subtle point: He substituted it for it and placed it where it stands and fills its place, to inform you that there is no difference between the absence of knowledge, which is ignorance, and the presence of a knowledge that does not go beyond this world. His saying ﴿outward from the life of this world﴾ indicates that this world has an outward and an inward. Its outward is what the ignorant know of enjoying its adornments and indulging in its pleasures. Its inward and reality is that it is a means to the Hereafter, from which one provisions oneself with obedience and righteous deeds. And ﴿they﴾ the second is an emphasis for ﴿they﴾ the first, or it is a subject. In making them manifest in either of the two cases, there is an alert to their heedlessness, in which they have become entangled and from which they never separate. And ﴿in themselves﴾ is the object of ﴿they reflect﴾, either with an omitted noun, that is, in the creation of themselves, so that they might emerge from heedlessness, know that they know only the outward of the life of this world, and draw evidence from that for the Creator, the Originator.

Then he informed, right after this, that the Truth is the reason for the creation of the heavens and the earth. Alternatively, ﴿in their own selves﴾ may be a complement (ẓarf) to the reflection on the creation of the heavens and the earth, so that "in their own selves" is an emphasis (ta'kid) of His saying "they reflect," as you would say, "See with your eye and hear with your ear." Al-Zamakhshari said: On this view it is as if He said: "Have they not reflected within themselves?" That is, in their hearts, which are empty of thought. Thought exists only in the hearts, but this is an added depiction of the state of those who reflect, like your saying, "Believe it in your heart and conceal it in your self." He also said: It may be the complement (ṣila) of the one who reflects, as in your saying, "He reflected on the matter and turned his thought over."

And ﴿what Allah created﴾ is connected to the omitted verb of speech. Its meaning is: "Have they not reflected, so that they would say this statement?" It was also said that its meaning is: "so that they would know," because the sentence contains an indication of it. End of quotation. The indication is His saying, "Have they not reflected?" It was also said: "Have they not reflected?" is connected to what follows it. Similar to this is: "then ﴿they reflect, [that] their companion has no madness﴾" (Al-A'raf: 184), and similar to it: ﴿and they thought that they had no escape﴾ (Fussilat: 48). Then "fi" would have the meaning of "bi" (with). Then "they reflect what is with their companion of madness" (Al-A'raf: 184) is as if He said: "Have they not reflected with their hearts, so that they would know?" End of quotation.

It is permissible that "tafakkaru" here be suspended (mu'allaqah), and its object is the clause from His saying "what Allah created" to its end. And ﴿in their own selves﴾ is a complement by way of emphasis, because thought exists only in the self, just as writing exists only by the hand. And ﴿with truth﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: it is accompanied by the truth and linked to it, and with an appointed term (ajal musamman) it must reach its end, which is the establishment of the Hour and the time of reckoning, reward and punishment. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 115). How He named their leaving unreturned to Him "vain." The meaning of "the meeting with their Lord" is the appointed term.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿except with truth﴾ means: by reason of the benefits which are a binding right, meaning from the indication to Him, worship of Him without slackness, the taking of lessons, benefits of kindness, and other things. ﴿And an appointed term﴾ is conjoined to "the truth," meaning: and with an appointed term, which is the Day of Resurrection. So in the verse there is an allusion to the Resurrection and the rising up, and the corruption of the structure of this world. Then He informed about many of the people that they disbelieved in that meaning, and He expressed it by "the meeting with Allah," because the meeting with Allah is the great matter, in which is salvation and destruction. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: Here He placed the proofs from the selves before the proofs from the horizons, while in ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in their own selves﴾ (Fussilat: 53) He placed the proofs of the horizons before the proofs of the selves. The wisdom of this is that the one who gives benefit mentions the benefit in the manner he chooses. If it is understood, well; otherwise he moves on to the clearer. The one who receives benefit first understands the clearer, then ascends to the more hidden. In "Have they not reflected?" the verb is attributed to the listener, so He began with what is understood first, then ascended to what is second. In ﴿We will show them﴾ (Fussilat: 53) He attributed it to the one who gives benefit, so He first mentioned the horizons; if they do not understand, then the selves, since a person is not oblivious to the proofs of the selves, unlike the proofs of the horizons, for he may be oblivious to them. This is observed in ﴿those who remember Allah standing and sitting﴾ (Al 'Imran: 191), etc. He began with the states of the selves, then with the proofs of the horizons. He also said here: "And indeed many," and before: "But most of the people," because here He mentioned "many" after mentioning the clear proofs, namely: ﴿Have they not reflected in their own selves﴾ and "what Allah created." Faith after the proofs is more than faith before them, so after mentioning the proof, a group of that majority must believe, and so the majority does not remain. End of quotation, and there is an abridgement in it. His first statement is only complete if "in their own selves" is taken as a place for reflection, and "what He created" is taken also as a second place.

﴿Have they not traveled in the land?﴾ This is a confirmation in the form of rebuke: that is, they have indeed traveled and looked at what befell those before them of the deniers of the messengers, and He described their state of strength, the tilling of the land and its cultivation, and that they were stronger than them in that. Mujahid said: ﴿and they tilled the land﴾ means they ploughed it. Al-Farra' said: they turned it over for cultivation. Others said: they turned the surface of the earth over to extract water, to extract minerals, and to cast seed into it for cultivation. And "ithara" (tilling) is moving a thing until its dust rises. Abu Ja'far read: "wa-ātharū al-arḍa," with a long vowel after the hamza. Ibn Mujahid said: That is nothing, and Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) explained it as lengthening of the vowel, like the line:

"And whoever blames time for one who has departed,"

and he said: it is due to poetic necessity and does not occur in the Qur'an. Al-Hasan (?) — rather, Abu Haywa read: "wa-āthirū," from al-atharah, which is monopolizing a thing. It was also read: "wa-athrū al-arḍa," meaning: they left traces of themselves upon it.

﴿And they built it﴾ from ʿimārah (cultivation/building), meaning: their staying in it was longer than the staying of these people; or from ʿumrān (settlement), meaning: they dwelt in it; or from ʿimārah. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿more than they built it﴾ refers to the building of the people of Makkah, and the people of Makkah are people of a valley without cultivation; they have no tilling of the land at all, nor any building whatsoever. So this is nothing but mockery of them and belittling of their state in their world, because most of what the people of the world rely upon and boast of is the matter of wealthy landowners (dahqana), and they too are weak in strength. ﴿So Allah would not have wronged them﴾: before it there is something omitted, meaning: they denied them, so they were destroyed. The two Ḥaramayn (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and Abu 'Amr read: "thumma kāna ʿāqibatu" with the nominative, as the subject of "kāna," and its predicate is "al-sūʾā," or it is the feminine of al-asʾa (the worst), from al-sūʾ (evil).

﴿That they denied﴾ is an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlihi) connected to the predicate, not to "asāʾa," for otherwise there would be a separation between the relative clause and its complement by the predicate, and that is not permitted. The meaning: then their end was, so the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun. ﴿The worst (al-sūʾā)﴾ means: the punishment which is the worst of punishments in the Hereafter, and it is Hell. It is also permissible that "al-sūʾā" be a verbal noun on the pattern fu'lā, like "al-ruj'ā," and be a predicate too. It is also permissible that it be an object of "asāʾa" in the sense of "they committed," and an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: the evil worst; and the predicate of "kāna" would be "an kadhdhabū." Al-A'mash and al-Hasan read: "al-sūwā," replacing the hamza with a waw and assimilating the waw into it, like the reading of the one who read "bi-l-sūwwi" with assimilation in (Surah) Yusuf. Ibn Mas'ud read: "al-sū'a," with masculine gender. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read: "ʿāqibata" with the accusative, as predicate of "kāna," and the noun is "al-sūʾā," or "al-sūʾa" as object, and "kadhdhabū" is the noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that "an" be in the sense of "ay" (that is): the explanation of the evil is the denial and mockery, and "kāna" is in the sense of "qāla," as in "nādā" and "kataba." Another possibility is that ﴿they committed the evil (asāʾū al-sūʾā)﴾ means: they committed the sin which is the worst of sins, and ﴿that they denied﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to it, and the predicate of "kāna" is omitted, as the answer of "lammā" and "law" is omitted for the purpose of vagueness. End of quotation. That "an" here is a particle of explanation (ḥarf tafsīr) is very forced. As for his phrase "al-khaṭāyāt" (the sins), it is so in the copy we consulted, pluralized with the broken plural with alif and ta', and that is not a regular pattern; it is only restricted to what is heard. It is not far that the addition of the ta' in "al-khaṭāyāt" comes from the copyist. As for his statement: "and ﴿that they denied﴾ is an explicative apposition to it, that is, to the worst, and the predicate of 'kāna' is omitted, etc." — this is a non-Arab understanding, because the sentence is independent and very good without omission, so one would have to invent an omitted element indicated by a sign. Our companions (the grammarians of our school) do not permit omitting the predicate of "kāna" and its sisters, either as a shortening or an abbreviation, except where something of it has been transmitted, and then it is not used as a general rule.

Abdullah and Talha read: "yubdi'u" with a dammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the dāl; the majority read it with a fatḥah. The two Abus (Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far?) read: "yurja'ūna" with the third-person yā'; the majority with the second-person tā', meaning: to His reward and His punishment. The majority read: ﴿yublisu﴾ with a kasrah on the lām; ʿAlī and al-Sulami read it with a fatḥah, from "abalsahu," when he silenced him. The majority read: "wa-lam yakun" with yā'; Kharija and al-Aris, both from Nafi', and Ibn Sinan from Abu Ja'far, and al-Antaki from Shayba, read with the feminine tā'.

﴿From their associates﴾ means: from those whom they worshipped besides Allah, and they are the idols, and they were attributed to them because they associated them in their wealth. It was said: because they took them, in their assumption, as partners of Allah. Muqatil said: the intended are the angels, intercessors with Allah, as they claimed: ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ (Al-Zumar: 3). ﴿And they will be﴾: its meaning is: and at their witnessing the command of Allah and the corruption of the state of the idols, He expressed it in the past tense to affirm the matter and the soundness of its occurrence. ﴿Al-sūʾā﴾ was written with an alif before the yā', as they wrote "ʿulamā'a Banī Isrā'īl" with a waw before the alif. The tanwin in ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is the tanwin of compensation for an omitted clause, meaning: ﴿and on the day the Hour is established﴾, the day when ﴿the criminals will be in despair﴾. The pronoun in ﴿they will be separated﴾ refers to the believers and the disbelievers, because of the indication of what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari said: It appears that it refers to what came before it, since before it is: ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾. Qatada said: it is a separation, with no reunion after it.

﴿In a garden (rawḍah)﴾: the rawḍah is land possessing plants and water. In the proverb: "more beautiful than an egg," meaning the eggs of the ostrich. The rawḍah is among the things that please the Arabs, and they have greatly praised it in their poetry.

﴿They will be made joyful (yuḥbarūn)﴾ means: they will be gladdened. Ḥabara-hu: he gladdened him with gladness, and his face brightened for him and its trace appeared upon him; yaḥburu with a ḍammah, ḥabran, ḥabratan, ḥubūran. In the proverb: "Their houses were filled with joy, so they await the tears." Al-Kisa'i related: "ḥabartuhu": I honored him and pampered him. ʿAlī ibn Sulayman said: it is from their saying: "there is a trace (ḥabrah) on his teeth," that is, a mark, meaning the trace of blessing flows over them. It was also said: from al-taḥbīr, which is beautification, meaning: they will be made beautiful. And it is said: "So-and-so has good ḥabr and sabr," with a fatḥah, when he is beautiful and of good appearance. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Mujahid said: they will be honored. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, al-Awza'i, and Waki' said: they will hear the songs. Abu Bakr and Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be crowned upon their heads. Ibn Kaysan said: they will be adorned. The meaning of ﴿brought forth (muḥḍarūn)﴾ is: gathered for it, none of them absent from it, by His saying: ﴿and they will not be out of it﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 37). The word "in a garden" came indefinite, and in the punishment definite. Al-Zamakhshari said: The indefiniteness is to suggest its unknown nature and magnify it. "Yuḥbarūn" came in the present verb form, because it is used for renewal, since every hour there comes to them what gladdens them of renewed delights of various kinds. "Muḥḍarūn" came in the active participle form, because it is used for permanence: so when they enter the punishment they remain in it as brought forth, and this is a necessary attribute of them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 30, verses 1–16 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 160] Surat al-Rum is Meccan.
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ ﴿in the nearest land. But after their defeat they will be victorious﴾ ﴿within a few years. The command belongs to God, before and after. On that day the believers will rejoice﴾ ﴿in God's victory. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿God's promise. God does not break His promise, but most people do not know﴾ ﴿They know the outward appearance of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves? God created the heavens and the earth and what is between them only with truth and for a specified term. Yet many people deny the meeting with their Lord﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen what was the end of those before them? They were stronger than them in power, and they ploughed the earth and cultivated it more than these have cultivated it. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. God would not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst evil: that they denied the signs of God and mocked them﴾ ﴿God originates creation, then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned﴾ ﴿On the day the Hour arises, the criminals will be dumbfounded﴾ ﴿They will have no intercessors from their associates, and they will disown their associates﴾ ﴿On the day the Hour arises, on that day they will be divided﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, they will be brought forth into the punishment﴾.

[p. 161] This surah is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyya and others said, without disagreement. Al-Zamakhshari said: except His saying: ﴿So glorified is God﴾ [al-Rum: 17].

Its occasion of revelation was that Kisra (the Persian king) sent an army against the Romans and appointed a man over them, and the narrators differed about his name. He marched against them with the people of Persia, prevailed, killed, destroyed, and cut down their olive trees. Their encounter took place at Adhri'at and Busra. Qaysar (the Byzantine emperor) had sent a man as commander over the Romans. Mujahid said: they met in al-Jazira. Al-Suddi said: in the land of Jordan and Palestine. This grieved the Muslims, because the Romans were People of the Book, and it pleased the polytheists, because the Persians (Majus) were not People of the Book. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) informed them that the Romans ﴿will be victorious within a few years﴾.

The first verses were revealed, and Abu Bakr proclaimed them in the outskirts of Mecca: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land. But after their defeat they will be victorious within a few years.﴾ Some of the polytheists of Quraysh said: Your companion claims that the Romans will defeat the Persians within a few years. Shall we wager on that with you? He said: Yes. This was before the prohibition of wagering (rihan). They agreed on a stake of a few years and three she-camels. Abu Bakr informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of this, and he said: "Why did you not make it bigger? Go back and increase them in the term and the wager." So they made the camels one hundred and the term nine years. The Romans prevailed over Persia in the seventh year. Among those who had wagered was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. When Abu Bakr wished to emigrate, Ubayy asked him for a guarantor for the wager in case the Romans won, and his son 'Abd al-Rahman guaranteed it. When Ubayy wished to go out to Uhud, 'Abd al-Rahman asked him for a guarantor, and he gave him one. Ubayy died from a wound that the Prophet (ﷺ) had inflicted on him. The Romans prevailed over Persia on the day of al-Hudaybiya. It was also said that the victory on the day of Badr was for both parties. Abu Bakr took the stake from the descendants of Ubayy and brought it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said to him: "Give it in charity."

The cause of the Romans' victory was that Kisra sent to Shahrayaz, who was the one he had appointed to fight the Romans, saying: "Kill your brother Farkhan for a statement he made, which was his saying: 'I saw myself sitting on the throne of Kisra.'" But he did not kill him. So Kisra sent to Persia that he had dismissed Shahrayaz and appointed his brother Farkhan, and wrote to him: when he takes office, he should kill his brother Shahrayaz. Farkhan intended to kill him, so Shahrayaz produced three letters from Kisra ordering him to kill his brother Farkhan. He said: "I have argued with you about your affair many times. Will you kill me on the strength of one letter?" So Farkhan returned the kingship to his brother. Shahrayaz wrote to Qaysar, the king of the Romans, and they cooperated against Kisra. The Romans defeated Persia, the news came, and the Muslims rejoiced. This was among the clear signs testifying to the authenticity of prophethood and that the Qur'an is from God, because it is a report of the unseen, which none knows except God.

Ali, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mu'awiya ibn Qurra and al-Hasan read ﴿ghulibat al-Rum﴾ with the verb active (ghalabat) and ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ with the verb passive (sayughlabun). The majority read ﴿ghulibat﴾ passive and ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ active. The interpretation of that, according to what Ibn 'Imran explained, is: the Romans were defeated in the nearest part of the countryside of Syria. By "rif" he means the cultivated land (al-sawad). This was also transmitted from Uthman. Abu Hatim interpreted it as: the Romans were defeated on the day of Badr, which was grievous to the disbelievers of Quraysh and pleased the believers, and God gave the good news to His servants that they would be victorious within a few years. End of quote. Thus he reports about the Romans that they have been defeated and that they will be victorious, so they were defeated twice. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reading with the ghayn vowelled with damma is more correct. People agreed on ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ with the ya vowelled with fatha, meaning the Romans. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he read "sayughlibun" with the ya vowelled with damma. In this reading the meaning transmitted by the reports is reversed. End of quote. His saying "they agreed" is not so. Do you not see that those who read "ghalabat" with fatha on the ghayn are the same ones who read "sayughlabun" with damma on the ya and fatha on the lam? And this reading is not specific to Ibn 'Umar. The majority read ﴿ghalabihim﴾ with fatha on the ghayn and the lam. Ali, Ibn 'Umar and Mu'awiya ibn Qurra read it with sukun. The analogous form from Ibn 'Umar would be "ghilabihim," on the pattern of "kitab."

[p. 162] The Rum: a group of Christians. "Adna al-ardh" means its nearest part. If the event took place at Adhri'at, then it is the nearest land in relation to Mecca, and this is what Imru' al-Qays mentioned in his saying:

I have looked upon it from Adhri'at, and its people are in Yathrib, the nearest of its dwellings with a high view.

If it was in al-Jazira, then it is nearest in relation to the land of Kisra. If it was in Jordan, then it is nearest in relation to the land of the Romans. Al-Kalbi read ﴿fi adna al-ardh﴾. The discussion of the meaning of "bid'" has already passed, in view of the two readings. So with "ghulibat," with damma on the ghayn, it is an idafa to the object; with fatha, it is an idafa to the subject, and the meaning is: the Muslims will defeat them within a few years, at the end of this period, which is the furthest extent of the meaning of "bid'."

The Muslims undertook jihad against the Romans. Our shaykh, the teacher Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, used to relate from Abu al-Hakam ibn Burjan that he derived from God's saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ up to His saying ﴿within a few years﴾ the conquest of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) by the Muslims, specifying its time and its day. At that time Jerusalem had come under Christian control. Ibn Burjan died before the time he had specified for the conquest, and after his death, after some time, the Muslims conquered it at the time Abu al-Hakam had specified. Abu Ja'far believed of this Abu al-Hakam that he would perceive some of the unseen matters, which he extracted from the Book of God.

﴿The command belongs to God﴾ means: the executing of rulings and their disposition as He wills. The majority read ﴿min qablu wa min ba'du﴾ with damma on both: that is, before the defeat of the Romans and after it. Since both are idafa to a definite noun and that noun is omitted, they are built on damma, and the discussion of this is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw). Abu al-Simmak, al-Jahdari and 'Awn al-'Uqayli read ﴿min qabl wa min ba'd﴾ with kasra and tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the genitive without assuming an omitted idafa, as if it were said: "qablan wa ba'dan," meaning "first and last." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: some Arabs say ﴿min qabl wa min ba'd﴾ with the genitive and tanwin. Al-Farra' said: it is also permissible to omit the tanwin, so that it remains as it is in idafa, even though the mudaf is omitted. End of quote. Al-Nahhas rejected what al-Farra' said, and said to al-Farra' in his book: there are many errors in the Qur'an in it, among them: he claimed that it is permissible to say "min qablu wa min ba'du," whereas it is only permissible to say "min qabl wa min ba'd" if they are indefinite, and the meaning is: from a previous one and from a later one. Al-Kisa'i reported from some of the Banu Asad: "lillahi al-amru min qablin wa min ba'du," the first genitive with tanwin, and the second with damma without tanwin.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is an adverbial complement of time for ﴿yafrahu al-mu'minun﴾ (the believers will rejoice), and on this meaning the exegetes explained it. It was also said: ﴿wa yawma'idhin﴾ is conjoined to ﴿min qablu wa min ba'du﴾, as if He had encompassed the three tenses: the past, the future and the present, and then began to report the rejoicing of the believers at the victory. And ﴿bi-nasr Allah﴾, that is, the Romans over Persia, or the Muslims over their enemy, or in the truth of what the Messenger (ﷺ) said, that the Romans will defeat Persia, or in that God empowers some of the wrongdoers over others until they destroy one another and turn away. These are possibilities. In a hadith: "Persia is a single blow or two blows, and there will be no Persia after them forever. The Romans are the people of horns; whenever one horn passes, another horn follows, until the end of time."

Ibn 'Abbas said: on the day of Badr was the defeat of the worshippers of idols and the worshippers of fire. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said the same. It was also said: news arrived on the day of al-Hudaybiya of the death of Kisra, and the Muslims rejoiced at the fighting of the polytheists and at the death of an enemy firmly established in the land. He is ﴿the Mighty﴾ in His vengeance upon His enemies, ﴿the Merciful﴾ to His friends. ﴿God's promise﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the previous sentence, which is His saying ﴿they will be victorious﴾ and His saying ﴿the believers will rejoice﴾.

﴿But most people﴾, the disbelievers of Quraysh and others, ﴿do not know﴾. He denied them knowledge that benefits for the Hereafter, while He affirmed for them knowledge of the affairs of this world. It was said: the meaning is that they do not know that affairs are from God, that His promise is not broken, and that what His Messenger (ﷺ) brings is true.

﴿They know the outward appearance﴾, that is, the manifest, which is what their senses perceive. It is as if their knowledge is merely the knowledge of animals. [p. 163] Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and the majority said: its meaning is what has manifestness and elevation in this world, such as the mastery of crafts and buildings, the places of earning wealth, agriculture, and the like. A group said: its meaning is what is passing and transient, that is, they know the affairs of this world, which has no permanence and no ultimate end. The poet al-Hudhali said:

The slanderers reproached her, saying I love her, and that is a complaint whose shame is manifestly removed from you.

That is, transient. Ibn Jubayr said: ﴿outward﴾ means they know it from the soothsayers, from what the devils steal. Al-Rummani said: whatever is known by the first sight is the outward, and whatever is known by the proof of reason is the inward. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they know﴾ is a substitute for ﴿they do not know﴾. In this substitution there is a subtle point: He substituted it for it and placed it where it stands and fills its place, to inform you that there is no difference between the absence of knowledge, which is ignorance, and the presence of a knowledge that does not go beyond this world. His saying ﴿outward from the life of this world﴾ indicates that this world has an outward and an inward. Its outward is what the ignorant know of enjoying its adornments and indulging in its pleasures. Its inward and reality is that it is a means to the Hereafter, from which one provisions oneself with obedience and righteous deeds. And ﴿they﴾ the second is an emphasis for ﴿they﴾ the first, or it is a subject. In making them manifest in either of the two cases, there is an alert to their heedlessness, in which they have become entangled and from which they never separate. And ﴿in themselves﴾ is the object of ﴿they reflect﴾, either with an omitted noun, that is, in the creation of themselves, so that they might emerge from heedlessness, know that they know only the outward of the life of this world, and draw evidence from that for the Creator, the Originator.

Then he informed, right after this, that the Truth is the reason for the creation of the heavens and the earth. Alternatively, ﴿in their own selves﴾ may be a complement (ẓarf) to the reflection on the creation of the heavens and the earth, so that "in their own selves" is an emphasis (ta'kid) of His saying "they reflect," as you would say, "See with your eye and hear with your ear." Al-Zamakhshari said: On this view it is as if He said: "Have they not reflected within themselves?" That is, in their hearts, which are empty of thought. Thought exists only in the hearts, but this is an added depiction of the state of those who reflect, like your saying, "Believe it in your heart and conceal it in your self." He also said: It may be the complement (ṣila) of the one who reflects, as in your saying, "He reflected on the matter and turned his thought over."

And ﴿what Allah created﴾ is connected to the omitted verb of speech. Its meaning is: "Have they not reflected, so that they would say this statement?" It was also said that its meaning is: "so that they would know," because the sentence contains an indication of it. End of quotation. The indication is His saying, "Have they not reflected?" It was also said: "Have they not reflected?" is connected to what follows it. Similar to this is: "then ﴿they reflect, [that] their companion has no madness﴾" (Al-A'raf: 184), and similar to it: ﴿and they thought that they had no escape﴾ (Fussilat: 48). Then "fi" would have the meaning of "bi" (with). Then "they reflect what is with their companion of madness" (Al-A'raf: 184) is as if He said: "Have they not reflected with their hearts, so that they would know?" End of quotation.

It is permissible that "tafakkaru" here be suspended (mu'allaqah), and its object is the clause from His saying "what Allah created" to its end. And ﴿in their own selves﴾ is a complement by way of emphasis, because thought exists only in the self, just as writing exists only by the hand. And ﴿with truth﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: it is accompanied by the truth and linked to it, and with an appointed term (ajal musamman) it must reach its end, which is the establishment of the Hour and the time of reckoning, reward and punishment. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 115). How He named their leaving unreturned to Him "vain." The meaning of "the meeting with their Lord" is the appointed term.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿except with truth﴾ means: by reason of the benefits which are a binding right, meaning from the indication to Him, worship of Him without slackness, the taking of lessons, benefits of kindness, and other things. ﴿And an appointed term﴾ is conjoined to "the truth," meaning: and with an appointed term, which is the Day of Resurrection. So in the verse there is an allusion to the Resurrection and the rising up, and the corruption of the structure of this world. Then He informed about many of the people that they disbelieved in that meaning, and He expressed it by "the meeting with Allah," because the meeting with Allah is the great matter, in which is salvation and destruction. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: Here He placed the proofs from the selves before the proofs from the horizons, while in ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in their own selves﴾ (Fussilat: 53) He placed the proofs of the horizons before the proofs of the selves. The wisdom of this is that the one who gives benefit mentions the benefit in the manner he chooses. If it is understood, well; otherwise he moves on to the clearer. The one who receives benefit first understands the clearer, then ascends to the more hidden. In "Have they not reflected?" the verb is attributed to the listener, so He began with what is understood first, then ascended to what is second. In ﴿We will show them﴾ (Fussilat: 53) He attributed it to the one who gives benefit, so He first mentioned the horizons; if they do not understand, then the selves, since a person is not oblivious to the proofs of the selves, unlike the proofs of the horizons, for he may be oblivious to them. This is observed in ﴿those who remember Allah standing and sitting﴾ (Al 'Imran: 191), etc. He began with the states of the selves, then with the proofs of the horizons. He also said here: "And indeed many," and before: "But most of the people," because here He mentioned "many" after mentioning the clear proofs, namely: ﴿Have they not reflected in their own selves﴾ and "what Allah created." Faith after the proofs is more than faith before them, so after mentioning the proof, a group of that majority must believe, and so the majority does not remain. End of quotation, and there is an abridgement in it. His first statement is only complete if "in their own selves" is taken as a place for reflection, and "what He created" is taken also as a second place.

﴿Have they not traveled in the land?﴾ This is a confirmation in the form of rebuke: that is, they have indeed traveled and looked at what befell those before them of the deniers of the messengers, and He described their state of strength, the tilling of the land and its cultivation, and that they were stronger than them in that. Mujahid said: ﴿and they tilled the land﴾ means they ploughed it. Al-Farra' said: they turned it over for cultivation. Others said: they turned the surface of the earth over to extract water, to extract minerals, and to cast seed into it for cultivation. And "ithara" (tilling) is moving a thing until its dust rises. Abu Ja'far read: "wa-ātharū al-arḍa," with a long vowel after the hamza. Ibn Mujahid said: That is nothing, and Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) explained it as lengthening of the vowel, like the line:

"And whoever blames time for one who has departed,"

and he said: it is due to poetic necessity and does not occur in the Qur'an. Al-Hasan (?) — rather, Abu Haywa read: "wa-āthirū," from al-atharah, which is monopolizing a thing. It was also read: "wa-athrū al-arḍa," meaning: they left traces of themselves upon it.

﴿And they built it﴾ from ʿimārah (cultivation/building), meaning: their staying in it was longer than the staying of these people; or from ʿumrān (settlement), meaning: they dwelt in it; or from ʿimārah. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿more than they built it﴾ refers to the building of the people of Makkah, and the people of Makkah are people of a valley without cultivation; they have no tilling of the land at all, nor any building whatsoever. So this is nothing but mockery of them and belittling of their state in their world, because most of what the people of the world rely upon and boast of is the matter of wealthy landowners (dahqana), and they too are weak in strength. ﴿So Allah would not have wronged them﴾: before it there is something omitted, meaning: they denied them, so they were destroyed. The two Ḥaramayn (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and Abu 'Amr read: "thumma kāna ʿāqibatu" with the nominative, as the subject of "kāna," and its predicate is "al-sūʾā," or it is the feminine of al-asʾa (the worst), from al-sūʾ (evil).

﴿That they denied﴾ is an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlihi) connected to the predicate, not to "asāʾa," for otherwise there would be a separation between the relative clause and its complement by the predicate, and that is not permitted. The meaning: then their end was, so the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun. ﴿The worst (al-sūʾā)﴾ means: the punishment which is the worst of punishments in the Hereafter, and it is Hell. It is also permissible that "al-sūʾā" be a verbal noun on the pattern fu'lā, like "al-ruj'ā," and be a predicate too. It is also permissible that it be an object of "asāʾa" in the sense of "they committed," and an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: the evil worst; and the predicate of "kāna" would be "an kadhdhabū." Al-A'mash and al-Hasan read: "al-sūwā," replacing the hamza with a waw and assimilating the waw into it, like the reading of the one who read "bi-l-sūwwi" with assimilation in (Surah) Yusuf. Ibn Mas'ud read: "al-sū'a," with masculine gender. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read: "ʿāqibata" with the accusative, as predicate of "kāna," and the noun is "al-sūʾā," or "al-sūʾa" as object, and "kadhdhabū" is the noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that "an" be in the sense of "ay" (that is): the explanation of the evil is the denial and mockery, and "kāna" is in the sense of "qāla," as in "nādā" and "kataba." Another possibility is that ﴿they committed the evil (asāʾū al-sūʾā)﴾ means: they committed the sin which is the worst of sins, and ﴿that they denied﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to it, and the predicate of "kāna" is omitted, as the answer of "lammā" and "law" is omitted for the purpose of vagueness. End of quotation. That "an" here is a particle of explanation (ḥarf tafsīr) is very forced. As for his phrase "al-khaṭāyāt" (the sins), it is so in the copy we consulted, pluralized with the broken plural with alif and ta', and that is not a regular pattern; it is only restricted to what is heard. It is not far that the addition of the ta' in "al-khaṭāyāt" comes from the copyist. As for his statement: "and ﴿that they denied﴾ is an explicative apposition to it, that is, to the worst, and the predicate of 'kāna' is omitted, etc." — this is a non-Arab understanding, because the sentence is independent and very good without omission, so one would have to invent an omitted element indicated by a sign. Our companions (the grammarians of our school) do not permit omitting the predicate of "kāna" and its sisters, either as a shortening or an abbreviation, except where something of it has been transmitted, and then it is not used as a general rule.

Abdullah and Talha read: "yubdi'u" with a dammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the dāl; the majority read it with a fatḥah. The two Abus (Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far?) read: "yurja'ūna" with the third-person yā'; the majority with the second-person tā', meaning: to His reward and His punishment. The majority read: ﴿yublisu﴾ with a kasrah on the lām; ʿAlī and al-Sulami read it with a fatḥah, from "abalsahu," when he silenced him. The majority read: "wa-lam yakun" with yā'; Kharija and al-Aris, both from Nafi', and Ibn Sinan from Abu Ja'far, and al-Antaki from Shayba, read with the feminine tā'.

﴿From their associates﴾ means: from those whom they worshipped besides Allah, and they are the idols, and they were attributed to them because they associated them in their wealth. It was said: because they took them, in their assumption, as partners of Allah. Muqatil said: the intended are the angels, intercessors with Allah, as they claimed: ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ (Al-Zumar: 3). ﴿And they will be﴾: its meaning is: and at their witnessing the command of Allah and the corruption of the state of the idols, He expressed it in the past tense to affirm the matter and the soundness of its occurrence. ﴿Al-sūʾā﴾ was written with an alif before the yā', as they wrote "ʿulamā'a Banī Isrā'īl" with a waw before the alif. The tanwin in ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is the tanwin of compensation for an omitted clause, meaning: ﴿and on the day the Hour is established﴾, the day when ﴿the criminals will be in despair﴾. The pronoun in ﴿they will be separated﴾ refers to the believers and the disbelievers, because of the indication of what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari said: It appears that it refers to what came before it, since before it is: ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾. Qatada said: it is a separation, with no reunion after it.

﴿In a garden (rawḍah)﴾: the rawḍah is land possessing plants and water. In the proverb: "more beautiful than an egg," meaning the eggs of the ostrich. The rawḍah is among the things that please the Arabs, and they have greatly praised it in their poetry.

﴿They will be made joyful (yuḥbarūn)﴾ means: they will be gladdened. Ḥabara-hu: he gladdened him with gladness, and his face brightened for him and its trace appeared upon him; yaḥburu with a ḍammah, ḥabran, ḥabratan, ḥubūran. In the proverb: "Their houses were filled with joy, so they await the tears." Al-Kisa'i related: "ḥabartuhu": I honored him and pampered him. ʿAlī ibn Sulayman said: it is from their saying: "there is a trace (ḥabrah) on his teeth," that is, a mark, meaning the trace of blessing flows over them. It was also said: from al-taḥbīr, which is beautification, meaning: they will be made beautiful. And it is said: "So-and-so has good ḥabr and sabr," with a fatḥah, when he is beautiful and of good appearance. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Mujahid said: they will be honored. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, al-Awza'i, and Waki' said: they will hear the songs. Abu Bakr and Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be crowned upon their heads. Ibn Kaysan said: they will be adorned. The meaning of ﴿brought forth (muḥḍarūn)﴾ is: gathered for it, none of them absent from it, by His saying: ﴿and they will not be out of it﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 37). The word "in a garden" came indefinite, and in the punishment definite. Al-Zamakhshari said: The indefiniteness is to suggest its unknown nature and magnify it. "Yuḥbarūn" came in the present verb form, because it is used for renewal, since every hour there comes to them what gladdens them of renewed delights of various kinds. "Muḥḍarūn" came in the active participle form, because it is used for permanence: so when they enter the punishment they remain in it as brought forth, and this is a necessary attribute of them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 30, verses 1–16 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 160] Surat al-Rum is Meccan.
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ ﴿in the nearest land. But after their defeat they will be victorious﴾ ﴿within a few years. The command belongs to God, before and after. On that day the believers will rejoice﴾ ﴿in God's victory. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿God's promise. God does not break His promise, but most people do not know﴾ ﴿They know the outward appearance of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves? God created the heavens and the earth and what is between them only with truth and for a specified term. Yet many people deny the meeting with their Lord﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen what was the end of those before them? They were stronger than them in power, and they ploughed the earth and cultivated it more than these have cultivated it. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. God would not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst evil: that they denied the signs of God and mocked them﴾ ﴿God originates creation, then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned﴾ ﴿On the day the Hour arises, the criminals will be dumbfounded﴾ ﴿They will have no intercessors from their associates, and they will disown their associates﴾ ﴿On the day the Hour arises, on that day they will be divided﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, they will be brought forth into the punishment﴾.

[p. 161] This surah is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyya and others said, without disagreement. Al-Zamakhshari said: except His saying: ﴿So glorified is God﴾ [al-Rum: 17].

Its occasion of revelation was that Kisra (the Persian king) sent an army against the Romans and appointed a man over them, and the narrators differed about his name. He marched against them with the people of Persia, prevailed, killed, destroyed, and cut down their olive trees. Their encounter took place at Adhri'at and Busra. Qaysar (the Byzantine emperor) had sent a man as commander over the Romans. Mujahid said: they met in al-Jazira. Al-Suddi said: in the land of Jordan and Palestine. This grieved the Muslims, because the Romans were People of the Book, and it pleased the polytheists, because the Persians (Majus) were not People of the Book. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) informed them that the Romans ﴿will be victorious within a few years﴾.

The first verses were revealed, and Abu Bakr proclaimed them in the outskirts of Mecca: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land. But after their defeat they will be victorious within a few years.﴾ Some of the polytheists of Quraysh said: Your companion claims that the Romans will defeat the Persians within a few years. Shall we wager on that with you? He said: Yes. This was before the prohibition of wagering (rihan). They agreed on a stake of a few years and three she-camels. Abu Bakr informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of this, and he said: "Why did you not make it bigger? Go back and increase them in the term and the wager." So they made the camels one hundred and the term nine years. The Romans prevailed over Persia in the seventh year. Among those who had wagered was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. When Abu Bakr wished to emigrate, Ubayy asked him for a guarantor for the wager in case the Romans won, and his son 'Abd al-Rahman guaranteed it. When Ubayy wished to go out to Uhud, 'Abd al-Rahman asked him for a guarantor, and he gave him one. Ubayy died from a wound that the Prophet (ﷺ) had inflicted on him. The Romans prevailed over Persia on the day of al-Hudaybiya. It was also said that the victory on the day of Badr was for both parties. Abu Bakr took the stake from the descendants of Ubayy and brought it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said to him: "Give it in charity."

The cause of the Romans' victory was that Kisra sent to Shahrayaz, who was the one he had appointed to fight the Romans, saying: "Kill your brother Farkhan for a statement he made, which was his saying: 'I saw myself sitting on the throne of Kisra.'" But he did not kill him. So Kisra sent to Persia that he had dismissed Shahrayaz and appointed his brother Farkhan, and wrote to him: when he takes office, he should kill his brother Shahrayaz. Farkhan intended to kill him, so Shahrayaz produced three letters from Kisra ordering him to kill his brother Farkhan. He said: "I have argued with you about your affair many times. Will you kill me on the strength of one letter?" So Farkhan returned the kingship to his brother. Shahrayaz wrote to Qaysar, the king of the Romans, and they cooperated against Kisra. The Romans defeated Persia, the news came, and the Muslims rejoiced. This was among the clear signs testifying to the authenticity of prophethood and that the Qur'an is from God, because it is a report of the unseen, which none knows except God.

Ali, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mu'awiya ibn Qurra and al-Hasan read ﴿ghulibat al-Rum﴾ with the verb active (ghalabat) and ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ with the verb passive (sayughlabun). The majority read ﴿ghulibat﴾ passive and ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ active. The interpretation of that, according to what Ibn 'Imran explained, is: the Romans were defeated in the nearest part of the countryside of Syria. By "rif" he means the cultivated land (al-sawad). This was also transmitted from Uthman. Abu Hatim interpreted it as: the Romans were defeated on the day of Badr, which was grievous to the disbelievers of Quraysh and pleased the believers, and God gave the good news to His servants that they would be victorious within a few years. End of quote. Thus he reports about the Romans that they have been defeated and that they will be victorious, so they were defeated twice. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reading with the ghayn vowelled with damma is more correct. People agreed on ﴿sayaghlibun﴾ with the ya vowelled with fatha, meaning the Romans. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he read "sayughlibun" with the ya vowelled with damma. In this reading the meaning transmitted by the reports is reversed. End of quote. His saying "they agreed" is not so. Do you not see that those who read "ghalabat" with fatha on the ghayn are the same ones who read "sayughlabun" with damma on the ya and fatha on the lam? And this reading is not specific to Ibn 'Umar. The majority read ﴿ghalabihim﴾ with fatha on the ghayn and the lam. Ali, Ibn 'Umar and Mu'awiya ibn Qurra read it with sukun. The analogous form from Ibn 'Umar would be "ghilabihim," on the pattern of "kitab."

[p. 162] The Rum: a group of Christians. "Adna al-ardh" means its nearest part. If the event took place at Adhri'at, then it is the nearest land in relation to Mecca, and this is what Imru' al-Qays mentioned in his saying:

I have looked upon it from Adhri'at, and its people are in Yathrib, the nearest of its dwellings with a high view.

If it was in al-Jazira, then it is nearest in relation to the land of Kisra. If it was in Jordan, then it is nearest in relation to the land of the Romans. Al-Kalbi read ﴿fi adna al-ardh﴾. The discussion of the meaning of "bid'" has already passed, in view of the two readings. So with "ghulibat," with damma on the ghayn, it is an idafa to the object; with fatha, it is an idafa to the subject, and the meaning is: the Muslims will defeat them within a few years, at the end of this period, which is the furthest extent of the meaning of "bid'."

The Muslims undertook jihad against the Romans. Our shaykh, the teacher Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, used to relate from Abu al-Hakam ibn Burjan that he derived from God's saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ up to His saying ﴿within a few years﴾ the conquest of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) by the Muslims, specifying its time and its day. At that time Jerusalem had come under Christian control. Ibn Burjan died before the time he had specified for the conquest, and after his death, after some time, the Muslims conquered it at the time Abu al-Hakam had specified. Abu Ja'far believed of this Abu al-Hakam that he would perceive some of the unseen matters, which he extracted from the Book of God.

﴿The command belongs to God﴾ means: the executing of rulings and their disposition as He wills. The majority read ﴿min qablu wa min ba'du﴾ with damma on both: that is, before the defeat of the Romans and after it. Since both are idafa to a definite noun and that noun is omitted, they are built on damma, and the discussion of this is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw). Abu al-Simmak, al-Jahdari and 'Awn al-'Uqayli read ﴿min qabl wa min ba'd﴾ with kasra and tanwin on both. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the genitive without assuming an omitted idafa, as if it were said: "qablan wa ba'dan," meaning "first and last." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: some Arabs say ﴿min qabl wa min ba'd﴾ with the genitive and tanwin. Al-Farra' said: it is also permissible to omit the tanwin, so that it remains as it is in idafa, even though the mudaf is omitted. End of quote. Al-Nahhas rejected what al-Farra' said, and said to al-Farra' in his book: there are many errors in the Qur'an in it, among them: he claimed that it is permissible to say "min qablu wa min ba'du," whereas it is only permissible to say "min qabl wa min ba'd" if they are indefinite, and the meaning is: from a previous one and from a later one. Al-Kisa'i reported from some of the Banu Asad: "lillahi al-amru min qablin wa min ba'du," the first genitive with tanwin, and the second with damma without tanwin.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is an adverbial complement of time for ﴿yafrahu al-mu'minun﴾ (the believers will rejoice), and on this meaning the exegetes explained it. It was also said: ﴿wa yawma'idhin﴾ is conjoined to ﴿min qablu wa min ba'du﴾, as if He had encompassed the three tenses: the past, the future and the present, and then began to report the rejoicing of the believers at the victory. And ﴿bi-nasr Allah﴾, that is, the Romans over Persia, or the Muslims over their enemy, or in the truth of what the Messenger (ﷺ) said, that the Romans will defeat Persia, or in that God empowers some of the wrongdoers over others until they destroy one another and turn away. These are possibilities. In a hadith: "Persia is a single blow or two blows, and there will be no Persia after them forever. The Romans are the people of horns; whenever one horn passes, another horn follows, until the end of time."

Ibn 'Abbas said: on the day of Badr was the defeat of the worshippers of idols and the worshippers of fire. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said the same. It was also said: news arrived on the day of al-Hudaybiya of the death of Kisra, and the Muslims rejoiced at the fighting of the polytheists and at the death of an enemy firmly established in the land. He is ﴿the Mighty﴾ in His vengeance upon His enemies, ﴿the Merciful﴾ to His friends. ﴿God's promise﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the previous sentence, which is His saying ﴿they will be victorious﴾ and His saying ﴿the believers will rejoice﴾.

﴿But most people﴾, the disbelievers of Quraysh and others, ﴿do not know﴾. He denied them knowledge that benefits for the Hereafter, while He affirmed for them knowledge of the affairs of this world. It was said: the meaning is that they do not know that affairs are from God, that His promise is not broken, and that what His Messenger (ﷺ) brings is true.

﴿They know the outward appearance﴾, that is, the manifest, which is what their senses perceive. It is as if their knowledge is merely the knowledge of animals. [p. 163] Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and the majority said: its meaning is what has manifestness and elevation in this world, such as the mastery of crafts and buildings, the places of earning wealth, agriculture, and the like. A group said: its meaning is what is passing and transient, that is, they know the affairs of this world, which has no permanence and no ultimate end. The poet al-Hudhali said:

The slanderers reproached her, saying I love her, and that is a complaint whose shame is manifestly removed from you.

That is, transient. Ibn Jubayr said: ﴿outward﴾ means they know it from the soothsayers, from what the devils steal. Al-Rummani said: whatever is known by the first sight is the outward, and whatever is known by the proof of reason is the inward. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they know﴾ is a substitute for ﴿they do not know﴾. In this substitution there is a subtle point: He substituted it for it and placed it where it stands and fills its place, to inform you that there is no difference between the absence of knowledge, which is ignorance, and the presence of a knowledge that does not go beyond this world. His saying ﴿outward from the life of this world﴾ indicates that this world has an outward and an inward. Its outward is what the ignorant know of enjoying its adornments and indulging in its pleasures. Its inward and reality is that it is a means to the Hereafter, from which one provisions oneself with obedience and righteous deeds. And ﴿they﴾ the second is an emphasis for ﴿they﴾ the first, or it is a subject. In making them manifest in either of the two cases, there is an alert to their heedlessness, in which they have become entangled and from which they never separate. And ﴿in themselves﴾ is the object of ﴿they reflect﴾, either with an omitted noun, that is, in the creation of themselves, so that they might emerge from heedlessness, know that they know only the outward of the life of this world, and draw evidence from that for the Creator, the Originator.

Then he informed, right after this, that the Truth is the reason for the creation of the heavens and the earth. Alternatively, ﴿in their own selves﴾ may be a complement (ẓarf) to the reflection on the creation of the heavens and the earth, so that "in their own selves" is an emphasis (ta'kid) of His saying "they reflect," as you would say, "See with your eye and hear with your ear." Al-Zamakhshari said: On this view it is as if He said: "Have they not reflected within themselves?" That is, in their hearts, which are empty of thought. Thought exists only in the hearts, but this is an added depiction of the state of those who reflect, like your saying, "Believe it in your heart and conceal it in your self." He also said: It may be the complement (ṣila) of the one who reflects, as in your saying, "He reflected on the matter and turned his thought over."

And ﴿what Allah created﴾ is connected to the omitted verb of speech. Its meaning is: "Have they not reflected, so that they would say this statement?" It was also said that its meaning is: "so that they would know," because the sentence contains an indication of it. End of quotation. The indication is His saying, "Have they not reflected?" It was also said: "Have they not reflected?" is connected to what follows it. Similar to this is: "then ﴿they reflect, [that] their companion has no madness﴾" (Al-A'raf: 184), and similar to it: ﴿and they thought that they had no escape﴾ (Fussilat: 48). Then "fi" would have the meaning of "bi" (with). Then "they reflect what is with their companion of madness" (Al-A'raf: 184) is as if He said: "Have they not reflected with their hearts, so that they would know?" End of quotation.

It is permissible that "tafakkaru" here be suspended (mu'allaqah), and its object is the clause from His saying "what Allah created" to its end. And ﴿in their own selves﴾ is a complement by way of emphasis, because thought exists only in the self, just as writing exists only by the hand. And ﴿with truth﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: it is accompanied by the truth and linked to it, and with an appointed term (ajal musamman) it must reach its end, which is the establishment of the Hour and the time of reckoning, reward and punishment. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 115). How He named their leaving unreturned to Him "vain." The meaning of "the meeting with their Lord" is the appointed term.
