The commentary begins with the first creation among these verses, which is the creation of man from dust, then his becoming a dispersed human race, which is a living creature from something inanimate. Then he followed this with His creating for him a spouse from himself, and affection was placed between them. That is a living creature from a living organ. He said: ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, because this is not perceived except by reflection on the joining together of two things that had no acquaintance between them. Then he followed it with what is witnessed by the whole world, which is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of languages and colours. Difference is among the necessary attributes of man that never leave him. He said: ﴿for those who know﴾, because it is a manifest sign to the whole world. Then he followed it with sleep and seeking (of provision), which are among the matters that are separable at some times, unlike the difference of tongues and colours. He said: ﴿for a people who hear﴾, because this is one of the acts of worship, and it might be supposed that it does not need a guide, so He drew attention to hearing, and made the heart's attention a matter of the guide's speech. When He mentioned the accidents of the souls, the necessary and the separable, He mentioned the separable accidents of the horizons, namely the showing of lightning and the sending down of rain. He placed them before what pertains to the earth, which is the bringing forth and the giving of life, just as He placed the heavens before the earth, and He placed the lightning before the sending down, because it is like the bearer of good news who comes before the one who arrives. The Bedouins do not know the grassy lands unless they have seen the lightning flashing from one side to the other. He said: ﴿for a people who understand﴾, because lightning and the sending down of rain are not a customary matter, so that one might imagine it to be a natural law, since it occurs in one town and not another, at one time and not another, and strongly or weakly. Therefore it is more evident to the intellect as an indication of the Agent who chooses, so He said: it is a sign for whoever understands, in that he does not reflect with complete reflection.

(p-169) Then He concluded these verses with the standing of the heavens and the earth, and that is among the necessary accidents, for each of the heaven and the earth does not depart from its place. So one marvels at the earth's standing firm and not falling, and at the height of the heaven and its stability without pillars. Then He followed that with the second creation, which is the coming forth from the earth. He mentioned from every category two matters: from the souls, "He created you and He created for you," and from the horizons, the heaven and the earth. From the necessary attributes of man are the difference of tongues and the difference of colours; from his particular properties are sleep and seeking; from the accidents of the horizons are the lightning and the rain; and from their necessary attributes is the standing of the heaven and the standing of the earth.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 30, verses 17–25 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon.﴾ ﴿He brings the living out of the dead, and brings the dead out of the living, and revives the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought out.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust, and then, behold, you are human beings dispersing.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves, that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the variation of your languages and your colours. Indeed in that are signs for those who know.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.﴾ ﴿And among His signs He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then when He calls you with one call from the earth, behold, you will come out.﴾

[p. 166] When the Exalted explained the immensity of His power in creating the heavens and the earth with truth, which is the state of the world's beginning, and their final destination to Paradise and Hellfire, which is the state of its end, He commanded the glorification of Him above every imperfection. The apparent meaning is that He commanded His servants to glorify Him at these times, because of the blessings that renew themselves in them. It may also be a metaphor for occupying the whole of the servant's time, so that he is always remembering his Lord and describing Him with what is due to Him in every state.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When He mentioned the promise and the threat, He followed it with a mention of what leads to the promise and saves from the threat. It has also been said that what is meant here by glorification (tasbih) is the prayer (salah). From Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah: maghrib, subh, 'asr and zuhr. As for 'isha', it is in His words ﴿and [part of] the night's hours﴾ [Hud: 114]. And from Ibn 'Abbas: the five prayers, and he took ﴿when you enter the evening﴾ to include maghrib and 'isha'.

﴿And to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraḍ, an interjected clause) between the two times. Its meaning is that praise is due from the inhabitants of the heavens and the inhabitants of the earth. Al-Hasan held that this verse is Medinan, because he used to say that the five prayers were prescribed in Medina. But most scholars said: rather, they were prescribed in Mecca. In al-Tahrir it is stated: the exegetes agreed that the five prayers are included in this verse. From Ibn 'Abbas: the five prayers are mentioned only in it.

He placed the evening (imsa') before the morning (isbah), as it was placed in His words ﴿He makes the night enter into the day﴾, and the darkness before the light. He paired imsa' with 'ashiyy (late afternoon) and isbah with izhar (noon), because each of them is followed by its counterpart: the late afternoon is followed by imsa', and the morning is followed by izhar. Since no verb is derived from 'ashiyy, one does not say a'sha, as one says amsa, asbaha and azhara, the construction (wa 'ashiyyan) was used.

'Ikrimah read: ﴿ḥīnan tumsūna wa-ḥīnan tuṣbiḥūna﴾ with tanwin on ḥīn, and the clause is then a qualifier (ṣifah) from which the returning pronoun has been omitted, its implied form being: you enter the evening in it and you enter the morning in it.

When He mentioned the originating and the returning, it was appropriate to mention ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾. The discussion of this verse has already been given in Surah Al 'Imran. ﴿And thus﴾ means: like that bringing out. The meaning is that the originating and the returning are equal with respect to Him, the Exalted. The majority read ﴿tukhrajūn﴾ with a dammah on the initial letter, in the passive voice. Ibn Wathhab, Talhah and al-A'mash read it with a fatḥah on the tā' of address and a ḍammah on the rā'.

Then the Exalted mentioned His signs from the beginning of the creation of man, sign by sign, up to the time of his resurrection from the grave. He said: ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾, He made their creation from dust, since He created their father Adam from dust. ﴿Dispersing (tantashirūn)﴾ means you move about to pursue your affairs. The particle ﴿then (thumma)﴾, which implies an interval and a delay, is used. The Exalted drew attention to the immensity of His power in creating man from dust, which is the furthest of things from the level of giving life, because it is cold and dry, while life is by heat and moisture. Likewise the spirit is luminous and light, while the body is heavy and still, and the animal moves toward the six directions. Thus dust is the furthest of all bodies from receiving life.

﴿From among yourselves (min anfusikum)﴾: there is a view regarding it, as in ﴿and from it He created its mate﴾ [al-Nisa: 1]. Either Eve was created from Adam's rib, or it means from your own kind and species. He gave the reason for creating spouses as tranquility with them, which is companionship (al-ilf). Whenever they are of the same kind, there is harmony between them, unlike two different kinds, between which there is aversion. This is also the wisdom in sending messengers from the race of the children of Adam. It is said: sakana ilayhi meaning he inclined to him, and from it comes al-sakan, a noun used in the sense of the object (maf'ul).

﴿Affection and mercy (mawaddatan wa-raḥmah)﴾, that is, between the spouses, after there had been no prior acquaintance that would require mutual affection. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ikrimah said: affection is sexual union (nikah), and mercy is offspring, and by these two He alluded to them. It was said: affection is for the young woman and mercy for the old woman. It was said: affection for the adult and mercy for the child. It was said: they are the bond of kinship (ishtibak al-raḥim). It was also said: affection is from God and hatred is from Satan.

﴿And the variation of your languages (ikhtilaf alsinatikum)﴾, that is, your tongues (lughat), so whoever has knowledge of many languages sees, in the variation of their structures or their rules while the meaning is one, wonders and marvels in both the simple and the compound words. From Wahb: the languages are seventy-two; seventeen belong to the descendants of Ham, nineteen to the descendants of Sam, and thirty-six to the descendants of Yafith. It was also said that what is meant by languages is sounds and tones. Al-Zamakhshari said: The tongues are the pleasures and the kinds and forms of the drops (nutaf). He, the Mighty and Majestic, made these things differ so that you can hardly hear two speakers agreeing in a single whisper or in loudness, sharpness or softness, in eloquence or in speech defect, in arrangement or in style, nor in other attributes and states of speech. End of quotation.

﴿And your colours (alwanikum)﴾: blackness, whiteness and other colours, and the kinds and types through the shaping of forms. Were it not for this variation, confusion would occur and many interests in dealings and other matters would be disrupted. In it there is a clear sign, since they branch out from one origin and differ in forms despite their multitude. The majority read ﴿lil-'ālamīn (for those who know)﴾ with a fatḥah on the lām, because it is itself a sign addressed to the world (al-'alam). Ḥafṣ, Ḥammad ibn Shu'ayb from Abu Bakr, 'Alqamah from 'Asim, and Yunus from Abu 'Amr read it with a kasrah on the lām, since those who benefit from it are only the people of knowledge, as in His words ﴿and none understands them except those of knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

The apparent meaning is that ﴿by night and by day﴾ is connected to ﴿your sleep (manamukum)﴾, and so the Exalted bestowed favour through this, since one may be active during the day, especially someone who is busy with his needs at night.

﴿And your seeking of His bounty (wabtighā'ukum min fadlihi)﴾, that is, in both of them, namely in the night and the day together, since some people seek their livelihood at night, such as travellers and watchmen, and others.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is from the rhetorical device of al-laff (wrapping, interweaving). Its arrangement is: ﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day and your seeking﴾. Because he separated the first two groups by the two others, which are two periods of time, and time and what occurs within it are like one thing, along with the aid that the interweaving gives to that. It is also permissible that ﴿your sleep﴾ is meant to cover both times, and ﴿your seeking of His bounty﴾ is also meant for both. The apparent meaning is the first, because it recurs in the Qur'an, and the most sound of meanings is what the Qur'an indicates. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Some exegetes said that there is an advancing and delaying in the speech (taqdim wa-ta'khir), but this is weak. What he meant is that the order of sleep is at night and seeking is for the day, and the wording of the verse does not indicate that.

﴿And among His signs He shows you the lightning (yurīkumu al-barq), as a fear and a hope﴾. Either ﴿among His signs﴾ is connected to ﴿He shows you﴾, so it occupies a position of accusative (naṣb), with min indicating the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah). Or ﴿He shows you﴾ is with an implied ''an'' (that), as the poet said:

*Ala ayyuhadhā al-zājirī uḥḍuru al-wagha*
*(Oh you who restrain me, let me attend the battle)*

Here uḥḍuru is in the nominative case, and the intended form is an uḥḍura. Since an was dropped, the verb took the nominative. This is not among the positions where an is dropped by analogy (qiyas). Or the verb is placed in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar) without its being used for that purpose, as al-Khalil said in one opinion:

*Urīdu li-ansā ḥubbahā*
*(I want to forget her love)*

That is, he (love) wanted me to forget her love. In both these two ways, the meaning is: ''And among His signs is His showing you the lightning''. Then ''min āyātihi'' is in the nominative position as the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada'). Al-Rummani said: It is possible that the intended meaning is: ''And among His signs He shows you lightning by means of them'', and it was omitted because min indicates it, as the poet said:

*Wa-mā al-dahru illā tāratān fa-minhumā*
*Amūtu wa-ukhrā abtaghī al-'aysha akdaḥu*
*(Time is only two occasions; of them one I die, and another I seek life, toiling)*

That is: of them one occasion I die. In all these three possibilities, min is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ).

﴿Fear and hope (khawfan wa-ṭama'an)﴾ are in the accusative as two verbal nouns in the position of the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), that is: fearful and hopeful. It was also said they are objects of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Al-Zajjaj said: Al-Zamakhshari permitted this on the assumption of the wish of fear and hope, so the subject is the same for the verb and the implied word, and it is not correct that the verb is yurikum, because the subject differs between the verb and the verbal noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: The objects are subjects in meaning, because they are the ones seeing it in its place, so it is as if it was said: He made you the seers of lightning, fearing and hoping. End of quotation. Whether it is a subject, some said: the causative hamzah (hamzat al-ta'diyah) does not establish for it the rule of the subject after it, and in this matter there is disagreement. The position of the majority is the requirement that the subject be the same (ittiḥad al-fā'il), and some grammarians do not require it. If it were said, according to the view of those who require it, that the implied meaning is: He shows you the lightning, and then you see it, fearing and hoping, and the verb is omitted for indication, that would be a valid parsing, and the subject would be the same.

Al-Dahhak said: fear of His thunderbolts, and hope for His rain. Qatadah said: fear for the traveller and hope for the one who stays at home. It was also said: fear that it will be dry (khulabb, lacking rain), and hope that it will be rainy. The poet said:

*Lā yakun barquka barqan khullaban*
*Inna khayra al-barqi mā al-ghaythu ma'ah*
*(Let not your lightning be a dry lightning; the best lightning is that which comes with rain)*

Ibn Salam said: fear of the cold that would destroy the crops, and hope for the rain that would give them life.

﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand﴾ (an taqūma): that they remain and are held up, like the phrase ''when darkness falls over them, they stand'', that is, they stay firm, by His command, that is, by His will. The first ''idhā'' is conditional, and the second ''idhā'' is for sudden occurrence and is the answer to the condition. The meaning is that your coming out at His call will not be delayed for the blink of an eye, just as the caller's summoned one responds to the obeyed master, as the poet said:

*Da'awtu Kulaybān da'watan fa-ka'annamā*
*Da'awtu qarīn al-ṭawdi aw huwa asra'u*
*(I called Kulayb with one call, as if I had called the echo of the mountain, or it is faster)*

Qarīn al-ṭawd means the echo, or the stone when it rolls. Al-ṭawd means the mountain. The call (da'wah) is the raising from the graves. ''From the earth (min al-arḍ)'' is connected to ''called you (da'ākum)'', and ''da'wah'' means one time, so there is no need to repeat your call because of the speed of the response. It was also said: ''from the earth'' is a qualifier of ''da'wah''. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: and ''min'' here, in my view, is for the end-point (intiha' al-ghayah), as one says: ''I called you from the mountain'' when the one called is on the mountain. End of quotation. That ''min'' indicates the end-point is an opinion rejected by our scholars. From Nafi' and Ya'qub: they stopped at ''da'wah'' and began with ''min al-arḍ''.

﴿When you come out (idhā antum takhrujūn)﴾: an ''alaq'' (governing element) from the earth is connected to ''takhrujūn'', and this is not permissible, because it would involve separating the condition from its answer, by stopping at ''da'wah'', and it would involve operating what follows the sudden ''idhā'' on what precedes it, which is not permitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: His words ''when He calls you'' are in the same position as His words ''He shows you'', in making the clause take the position of a singular noun in meaning, as if it was said: ''And among His signs is the standing of the heavens and the earth, then the coming out of the dead from the graves when He calls them with one call: O people of the graves, come out!'' He linked this to the standing of the heavens and the earth with ''thumma'', to explain the greatness of that matter and His power over its like, which is to say: O people of the graves, stand up! Then not one soul of the first and the last will remain except that it stands looking. End of quotation. Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i read ''takhrujūn'' with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the rā'. The rest of the seven read it with a ḍammah on the tā' and a fatḥah on the rā'.

The commentary begins with the first creation among these verses, which is the creation of man from dust, then his becoming a dispersed human race, which is a living creature from something inanimate. Then he followed this with His creating for him a spouse from himself, and affection was placed between them. That is a living creature from a living organ. He said: ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, because this is not perceived except by reflection on the joining together of two things that had no acquaintance between them. Then he followed it with what is witnessed by the whole world, which is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of languages and colours. Difference is among the necessary attributes of man that never leave him. He said: ﴿for those who know﴾, because it is a manifest sign to the whole world. Then he followed it with sleep and seeking (of provision), which are among the matters that are separable at some times, unlike the difference of tongues and colours. He said: ﴿for a people who hear﴾, because this is one of the acts of worship, and it might be supposed that it does not need a guide, so He drew attention to hearing, and made the heart's attention a matter of the guide's speech. When He mentioned the accidents of the souls, the necessary and the separable, He mentioned the separable accidents of the horizons, namely the showing of lightning and the sending down of rain. He placed them before what pertains to the earth, which is the bringing forth and the giving of life, just as He placed the heavens before the earth, and He placed the lightning before the sending down, because it is like the bearer of good news who comes before the one who arrives. The Bedouins do not know the grassy lands unless they have seen the lightning flashing from one side to the other. He said: ﴿for a people who understand﴾, because lightning and the sending down of rain are not a customary matter, so that one might imagine it to be a natural law, since it occurs in one town and not another, at one time and not another, and strongly or weakly. Therefore it is more evident to the intellect as an indication of the Agent who chooses, so He said: it is a sign for whoever understands, in that he does not reflect with complete reflection.

(p-169) Then He concluded these verses with the standing of the heavens and the earth, and that is among the necessary accidents, for each of the heaven and the earth does not depart from its place. So one marvels at the earth's standing firm and not falling, and at the height of the heaven and its stability without pillars. Then He followed that with the second creation, which is the coming forth from the earth. He mentioned from every category two matters: from the souls, "He created you and He created for you," and from the horizons, the heaven and the earth. From the necessary attributes of man are the difference of tongues and the difference of colours; from his particular properties are sleep and seeking; from the accidents of the horizons are the lightning and the rain; and from their necessary attributes is the standing of the heaven and the standing of the earth.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 30, verses 26–32 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ ﴿It is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and it is easier for Him. To Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you, sharing equally in it, so that you fear them as you fear one another? Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason.﴾ ﴿But those who wronged follow their desires without knowledge. So who can guide those whom Allah has led astray? For them there are no helpers.﴾ ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a people inclining to truth, the nature (fitra) of Allah upon which He created mankind. There is no altering the creation of Allah. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿Turning penitently to Him, and fear Him, and establish prayer, and do not be among the polytheists,﴾ ﴿of those who have divided their religion and become sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has.﴾

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is general, encompassing all of them being under His dominion and subjugation. Al-Hasan said: "qanitun" means standing as witnesses to His oneness, as the poet said:

*"And in everything there is a sign that indicates that He is One."*

Ibn 'Abbas said: "obedient," i.e., in His disposing of them, none of them can resist Him in what He wills to do to them, of life and death, health and sickness. This is obedience of will, not obedience of worship. It was also said: "standing" on the Day of Resurrection, the day when people will stand before the Lord of the worlds. If *qunut* is taken to mean sincerity, as Ibn Jubayr said, or acknowledgment of servitude, or that "devoutly obedient" refers to both angels and believers, then this is because every general statement is subject to specification.

﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: i.e., repetition is easier for Him. *Ahwan* here is not an elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*, the comparative/superlative pattern), because there is no gradation with Allah between the two states of origination and repetition. Therefore Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym interpreted it to mean *hayyin* ("easy"). Likewise it is so in the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud). The pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to Allah. It was also said that *ahwan* is comparative, according to human belief and what observation shows them, that repetition of many things is easier than initial creation, since it does not require the deliberation that initial creation required. Although, for Him, both are equally easy. It was also said that the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to creation, meaning: repetition is easier for creatures, i.e., quicker, because initial creation involves gradual progression from stage to stage until one becomes a human being, whereas repetition does not need these gradual stages of development. Allah simply calls, and they emerge. So it is as if He said: "It is easier for Him," i.e., shorter in duration and less in transition. It was also said that the meaning is: "it is easier for the created being," i.e., one who recreates something after having originated it. This is the custom of created beings, so how do you deny repetition in the case of the Creator? Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In my view, the more apparent is that the pronoun refers to Allah, and this is supported by His words: ﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness﴾, as it came in a wording that contains a seeking of refuge and a drawing of evidence from the created being regarding the Creator, and a comparison with what people know of themselves. The aspect of greatness is pure, in that He is given the highest likeness, which is not connected to Him. How could there be any likeness, when nothing is like Him?" End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why was the complement delayed in His words ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ but placed first in His words ﴿it is easy for Me﴾ [Maryam 19:9]? I say: there, exclusivity was intended, namely His overpowering, so it was said: "it is easy for Me," even though it is difficult in your view, even if it was born between an aged man and a barren woman. Here, however, there is no sense of exclusivity, especially since the matter is based on what they understand, that repetition is easier than initial creation. If the complement had been placed first, the meaning would have changed. End of quote. The basis of his statement is that fronting an element of the sentence indicates exclusivity, and we have discussed this with him and did not accept it in His words: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:5].

﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness﴾: It was said that this is connected to what precedes it, as al-Zajjaj said, namely His words ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾; He has set for you a parable in what is easy or difficult. It was also said that it is connected to what follows it, namely His words ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves.﴾ It was also said: the parable (*mathal*) is the most exalted, highest attribute, which no other shares, namely that He is the One capable who is not unable to do anything, whether origination, repetition, or anything else. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: i.e., the Subduer of everything, ﴿the Wise﴾ whose acts follow the requirement of His wisdom. It is reported from Mujahid that "the highest likeness" is the statement: "There is no god but Allah," and that to Him belongs the attribute of oneness. This is supported by His words ﴿He has coined for you﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and others said: Allah clarified the matter of the idols and the corruption of the belief of those who associate them with Allah, by His coining this parable. Its meaning is: O people, if you have slaves whom you own, you do not make them partners in your wealth and important affairs, nor in anything on the basis of equal standing, nor is it proper for you to fear them lest they inherit your wealth or divide it with you during your lifetime, as some of you do with others. If this is so among you, how can you say that among His slaves and His possessions there are partners in His authority and divinity, and attribute to Him what you do not find fitting for yourselves? This meaning came in the form of a question and affirmation. Al-Suddi said: They used to make their gods inherit, so this was revealed. It was also said: when this was revealed, the people of Mecca said: "That will never be!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then why is it permitted for your Lord?"

The *min* in ﴿from yourselves﴾ indicates the starting point, as if He said: He took a parable and drew it from the nearest thing to you, namely yourselves, and this is not far-fetched. The *min* in ﴿among what﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] indicates partitive meaning. The *min* in ﴿partners﴾ is extra, for emphasizing the interrogative that functions as a negation. It means: none of you is pleased that his slave should share with him in his property, his wife, or what belongs exclusively to him, to the point of being his equal. How, then, would you accept a partner for Allah, while He is the Lord of lords and the Owner of both free people and slaves?

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: There is similarity and dissimilarity between the parable and what it parables. The similarity is known, and the dissimilarity is in several respects. His words ﴿from yourselves﴾ mean from your own offspring, together with the lowliness, deficiency, and weakness of the self, while He compared Himself to you despite His greatness, majesty, and power. His words ﴿among what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] mean your slaves. Ownership is that which precedes transfer by sale and cessation by manumission, and what Allah owns never leaves His ownership. So if your slave may not share with you, though he is like you in every respect and like you in humanity, in the state of slavery, how could a slave share with Allah in every respect, when He is utterly separate from him? His words ﴿in what We have provided for you﴾ mean that the true provider for you is Allah, and the provision is truly from Him. If it is not permitted for a slave to share with you in what is yours in name, how could He have a partner in what truly belongs to Him? End of quote, with some summarizing. The word ﴿partners﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject of the nominal sentence, and ﴿in what We have provided for you﴾ is connected to it, and ﴿for you﴾ is the predicate. ﴿Among what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), because it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun placed before it, and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and the governing element of it is the governing element of the prepositional phrase, which functions as the predicate, and it is understood after the subject. The *ma* in ﴿what We have provided﴾ refers to the category, and the meaning is: are there partners in what We have provided for you who are of the category that your right hands possess, who belong to you? It is also permitted that ﴿for you﴾ be connected to ﴿partners﴾ and that ﴿of what We have provided for you﴾ be the predicate, as you say: "For Zayd in Medina there is one who hates," so "for Zayd" is connected to "one who hates," which is the subject, and "in Medina" is the predicate. The sentence ﴿so you are in it equal﴾ is in the position of the answer to the interrogative that implies negation, and ﴿in it﴾ is connected to ﴿equal﴾. ﴿You fear them﴾ is a second predicate for ﴿you﴾, and the meaning is: "So you are equal with them in what We have provided for you, you fear them as some of you fear others, O masters." The purpose is to negate partnership, equality, and fear, and the negation does not apply only to the answer and what follows it, as in one of the two readings of: "Will you not come to us and speak to us?" That is, "You do not come to us and speak to us," meaning you come and do not speak. Rather, it is according to the other reading: "Will you not come to us, so how will you speak to us?" That is, there is no coming from you, so there is no speaking. Likewise here: they have no partner, so there is no equality and no fear.

The majority read ﴿fear them﴾ with the accusative (*nasb*), with the verbal noun (*masdar*) annexed to its subject; Ibn Abi 'Ubayda read it in the nominative, with the verbal noun annexed to its object. Both are good readings, and there is no impropriety in annexing a verbal noun to its object while the subject is present.

﴿Thus﴾: i.e., like that clarification, ﴿We detail the signs﴾: i.e., We make them clear, because the parable reveals meanings and makes them plain, as it is like a depiction and a shaping of them. Do you not see how He depicted polytheism in a disfigured form? The majority read ﴿We detail﴾ with *nun* (the first-person plural), in agreement with ﴿We have provided﴾. 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Umar, read it with *ya'* of the third person, in consideration of ﴿He has coined﴾, since it is attributed to the third person. Some scholars cited this verse as evidence for the validity of the principle of partnership among created beings, because some depend on others. It is as if He said: what is forbidden and considered abhorrent is the partnership of slaves with their masters; but the partnership of masters with one another is not forbidden nor abhorrent. The transition with *bal* ("but") in His words ﴿But those who wronged follow﴾ came in accordance with what the verse contains, since the meaning is: they have no proof or excuse for their associating others with Allah; rather, it is merely following desire without knowledge, because a person may have a desire while knowing (that it is wrong). ﴿Those who wronged﴾ are the polytheists, who followed their desires, ignorant and wandering aimlessly, not restrained from their desires by knowledge, since they are free of the knowledge that could deter one who follows desire.

﴿So who can guide those whom Allah has led astray?﴾: i.e., no one can guide those whom Allah has led astray; these are among those whom Allah has led astray, so there is no guide for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whom Allah has led astray" means whom Allah has forsaken and not shown kindness to, because He knows that he is one to whom no kindness is extended, from among those whom He could guide, like him. ﴿For them there are no helpers﴾ is evidence that "leading astray" means "forsaking." End of quote, and this is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school).

﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾: i.e., straighten your face toward it, turn to it without looking aside. This is a figure of speech for his turning to the religion, adhering to it, steadfastness in it, and concern for its causes. When a person is concerned with something, he fixes his gaze on it and straightens his face toward it, facing it. The religion is the religion of Islam. The face is mentioned because it gathers the human senses and is the most noble of them. *Hanifan* ("inclining to truth") is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in *aqim* (the imperative "set"), or from "face," or from "religion." Its meaning is: turning away from the altered and abrogated (*mansukha*) religions.

﴿The nature (fitra) of Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, like His words ﴿the coloring of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara 2:138]. It was also said that it is in the accusative by an elided verb whose estimated form is: "hold fast to the nature of Allah." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Adhere to the nature of Allah," or "upon you is the nature of Allah." It was made elided because of the address to the plural, in agreement with His words ﴿turning penitently to Him﴾, where "turning penitently" is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "adhere." The phrase "and establish" and "and do not be" is conjoined to this elided element. End of quote. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿so set your face﴾ is "so set your faces," and it is not specific to the Messenger alone. It seems to be an address to a singular addressee intended to mean the plural, i.e., "so set (yourselves), O addressee," and then the plural is used according to meaning, because a single addressee is not intended. If this is the case, then "turning penitently," "and establish," and "and do not be" carry the sense of the plural. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "or upon you is the nature of Allah," is not permissible, because it involves omitting the word of warning (*ighra'*, the word "upon you," *'alayka*), and it is not permissible to omit it, since the verb has been omitted and "upon you" has been put in its place. If its omission were allowed, it would be a serious imbalance, since it would involve omitting both the substitute and that for which it substitutes.

Al-Fitra (the innate disposition) is said to be the religion of Islam, and "al-nas" (the people) is restricted to the believers. It is also said to be the covenant that God took from the descendants of Adam when He brought them forth from his loins as particles (nasam). The skilled scholars (al-hudhdhaq) preferred that it is the capacity present in the child to reflect upon God's creatures and to infer from them their Originator, so that he believes in Him and follows His laws. However, there may arise external factors that divert him from this, such as his parents making him a Jew or a Christian, and the seduction of the devils of mankind and jinn.

﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾, i.e., there is no alteration of this capacity on the part of the Creator. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd said: there is no alteration of the religion of God, meaning: of the creeds of the religions, since they agree on this. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it is not fitting that this innate disposition be changed or altered. Ibn Abbas said: there is no alteration of God's decree concerning their happiness and misery. It is also said that it is a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, i.e., do not alter that religion. It is also said: ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ in the sense that monotheism is inherent in it, with no change in it, so that even if you asked him, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", he would say, "God." What is reported from Ibn Abbas, that the meaning of ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ is a prohibition against castrating male animals, is strange. The view of one who holds that the meaning of this sentence is a rebuttal of the disbelievers, inserted parenthetically into the speech, as if he were saying: "Establish your face for the religion which has such-and-such attributes, for these disbelievers, and those whom God has created for disbelief..." and ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾, meaning: they do not prosper; that which you were commanded to set your face toward is the religion that is most thorough in uprightness, is also mentioned as an objection. The word al-qayyim (the upright) is an intensive form with the ya', from al-qiyam, in the sense of uprightness. Its pattern is faʻil; its original form is qaywim, like yad; the ya' and waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into ya', and the ya' was assimilated into it. This pattern is specific to hollow-medial roots, and in the sound (non-weak) roots there has come from it only bay'is and sayqal, a proper name for a woman.

(Muniban) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (al-nas), especially if by al-nas is meant the believers; or from the pronoun in "Adhere to the fitra of God"; and this is al-Zamakhshari's estimation; or from the pronoun in "(fa-aqim)", since the intended addressee is the Messenger ﷺ and his community, and it is as if a coordinated element has been omitted, i.e., "establish your face and your community." Al-Zajjaj likewise claimed this regarding ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], i.e., "O Prophet and people." What points to this is the circumstantial clause (muniban) being in the plural, and in ﴿when you divorce﴾ [al-Talaq: 1] the address is in the plural both there and in what follows. Or it is the predicate of an elided kana, i.e., "be penitent," and what points to it is his later saying (wa-la takunu, "and do not be"). These are all transmitted possibilities. (Min al-mushrikin) means "from among the Jews and Christians," as said by Qatada. Ibn Zayd said: they are the Jews. From Abu Hurayrah and Aisha: they are the people of the qibla. The term of association (ishrak), according to this, is used figuratively, since they became sects in their religion. The apparent meaning is that the mushrikun are everyone who associates partners with God, so the People of the Book and others are included among them. (Min alladhina) is a substitute (badal) for (al-mushrikin). ﴿Who split up their religion﴾, i.e., the religion of Islam, and made it into different religions according to the differences of their desires.

﴿And became sects﴾: each group follows its leader, who was the cause of its misguidance.

﴿Every party﴾, i.e., of them, is pleased with its own doctrine and captivated by it. The apparent view is that ﴿every party﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and (farihun, "rejoicing") is the predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that (min alladhina) is disconnected from what precedes it, and its meaning is: "of those who abandon their religion, every party rejoicing in what they have." But he put (farihun) in the nominative as a description of (kull), as in his saying:

"And every friend is not one who humbles his own self"

End of his words. He first estimated (farihin) as genitive, an adjective of hizb, then said: but it was put in the nominative as a description of (kull), because when you say, "From your people is every righteous man (kull rajul salih)," it is permissible for "salih" to be in the genitive as an adjective of "rajul," which is the more common, as in his saying:

"Every abundant eye poured upon him, so they left every garden like a dirham"

and it is permissible to make it nominative as an adjective of (kull), as in his saying:

"And upon him blew every turbulent wind, wild, which has no mind to its reason"

where "hawja'" (wild) is in the nominative as an adjective of "kull."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 30, verses 26–32 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ ﴿It is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and it is easier for Him. To Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you, sharing equally in it, so that you fear them as you fear one another? Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason.﴾ ﴿But those who wronged follow their desires without knowledge. So who can guide those whom Allah has led astray? For them there are no helpers.﴾ ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a people inclining to truth, the nature (fitra) of Allah upon which He created mankind. There is no altering the creation of Allah. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿Turning penitently to Him, and fear Him, and establish prayer, and do not be among the polytheists,﴾ ﴿of those who have divided their religion and become sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has.﴾

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is general, encompassing all of them being under His dominion and subjugation. Al-Hasan said: "qanitun" means standing as witnesses to His oneness, as the poet said:

*"And in everything there is a sign that indicates that He is One."*

Ibn 'Abbas said: "obedient," i.e., in His disposing of them, none of them can resist Him in what He wills to do to them, of life and death, health and sickness. This is obedience of will, not obedience of worship. It was also said: "standing" on the Day of Resurrection, the day when people will stand before the Lord of the worlds. If *qunut* is taken to mean sincerity, as Ibn Jubayr said, or acknowledgment of servitude, or that "devoutly obedient" refers to both angels and believers, then this is because every general statement is subject to specification.

﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: i.e., repetition is easier for Him. *Ahwan* here is not an elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*, the comparative/superlative pattern), because there is no gradation with Allah between the two states of origination and repetition. Therefore Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym interpreted it to mean *hayyin* ("easy"). Likewise it is so in the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud). The pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to Allah. It was also said that *ahwan* is comparative, according to human belief and what observation shows them, that repetition of many things is easier than initial creation, since it does not require the deliberation that initial creation required. Although, for Him, both are equally easy. It was also said that the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to creation, meaning: repetition is easier for creatures, i.e., quicker, because initial creation involves gradual progression from stage to stage until one becomes a human being, whereas repetition does not need these gradual stages of development. Allah simply calls, and they emerge. So it is as if He said: "It is easier for Him," i.e., shorter in duration and less in transition. It was also said that the meaning is: "it is easier for the created being," i.e., one who recreates something after having originated it. This is the custom of created beings, so how do you deny repetition in the case of the Creator? Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In my view, the more apparent is that the pronoun refers to Allah, and this is supported by His words: ﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness﴾, as it came in a wording that contains a seeking of refuge and a drawing of evidence from the created being regarding the Creator, and a comparison with what people know of themselves. The aspect of greatness is pure, in that He is given the highest likeness, which is not connected to Him. How could there be any likeness, when nothing is like Him?" End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why was the complement delayed in His words ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ but placed first in His words ﴿it is easy for Me﴾ [Maryam 19:9]? I say: there, exclusivity was intended, namely His overpowering, so it was said: "it is easy for Me," even though it is difficult in your view, even if it was born between an aged man and a barren woman. Here, however, there is no sense of exclusivity, especially since the matter is based on what they understand, that repetition is easier than initial creation. If the complement had been placed first, the meaning would have changed. End of quote. The basis of his statement is that fronting an element of the sentence indicates exclusivity, and we have discussed this with him and did not accept it in His words: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:5].

﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness﴾: It was said that this is connected to what precedes it, as al-Zajjaj said, namely His words ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾; He has set for you a parable in what is easy or difficult. It was also said that it is connected to what follows it, namely His words ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves.﴾ It was also said: the parable (*mathal*) is the most exalted, highest attribute, which no other shares, namely that He is the One capable who is not unable to do anything, whether origination, repetition, or anything else. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: i.e., the Subduer of everything, ﴿the Wise﴾ whose acts follow the requirement of His wisdom. It is reported from Mujahid that "the highest likeness" is the statement: "There is no god but Allah," and that to Him belongs the attribute of oneness. This is supported by His words ﴿He has coined for you﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and others said: Allah clarified the matter of the idols and the corruption of the belief of those who associate them with Allah, by His coining this parable. Its meaning is: O people, if you have slaves whom you own, you do not make them partners in your wealth and important affairs, nor in anything on the basis of equal standing, nor is it proper for you to fear them lest they inherit your wealth or divide it with you during your lifetime, as some of you do with others. If this is so among you, how can you say that among His slaves and His possessions there are partners in His authority and divinity, and attribute to Him what you do not find fitting for yourselves? This meaning came in the form of a question and affirmation. Al-Suddi said: They used to make their gods inherit, so this was revealed. It was also said: when this was revealed, the people of Mecca said: "That will never be!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then why is it permitted for your Lord?"

The *min* in ﴿from yourselves﴾ indicates the starting point, as if He said: He took a parable and drew it from the nearest thing to you, namely yourselves, and this is not far-fetched. The *min* in ﴿among what﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] indicates partitive meaning. The *min* in ﴿partners﴾ is extra, for emphasizing the interrogative that functions as a negation. It means: none of you is pleased that his slave should share with him in his property, his wife, or what belongs exclusively to him, to the point of being his equal. How, then, would you accept a partner for Allah, while He is the Lord of lords and the Owner of both free people and slaves?

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: There is similarity and dissimilarity between the parable and what it parables. The similarity is known, and the dissimilarity is in several respects. His words ﴿from yourselves﴾ mean from your own offspring, together with the lowliness, deficiency, and weakness of the self, while He compared Himself to you despite His greatness, majesty, and power. His words ﴿among what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] mean your slaves. Ownership is that which precedes transfer by sale and cessation by manumission, and what Allah owns never leaves His ownership. So if your slave may not share with you, though he is like you in every respect and like you in humanity, in the state of slavery, how could a slave share with Allah in every respect, when He is utterly separate from him? His words ﴿in what We have provided for you﴾ mean that the true provider for you is Allah, and the provision is truly from Him. If it is not permitted for a slave to share with you in what is yours in name, how could He have a partner in what truly belongs to Him? End of quote, with some summarizing. The word ﴿partners﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject of the nominal sentence, and ﴿in what We have provided for you﴾ is connected to it, and ﴿for you﴾ is the predicate. ﴿Among what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), because it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun placed before it, and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and the governing element of it is the governing element of the prepositional phrase, which functions as the predicate, and it is understood after the subject. The *ma* in ﴿what We have provided﴾ refers to the category, and the meaning is: are there partners in what We have provided for you who are of the category that your right hands possess, who belong to you? It is also permitted that ﴿for you﴾ be connected to ﴿partners﴾ and that ﴿of what We have provided for you﴾ be the predicate, as you say: "For Zayd in Medina there is one who hates," so "for Zayd" is connected to "one who hates," which is the subject, and "in Medina" is the predicate. The sentence ﴿so you are in it equal﴾ is in the position of the answer to the interrogative that implies negation, and ﴿in it﴾ is connected to ﴿equal﴾. ﴿You fear them﴾ is a second predicate for ﴿you﴾, and the meaning is: "So you are equal with them in what We have provided for you, you fear them as some of you fear others, O masters." The purpose is to negate partnership, equality, and fear, and the negation does not apply only to the answer and what follows it, as in one of the two readings of: "Will you not come to us and speak to us?" That is, "You do not come to us and speak to us," meaning you come and do not speak. Rather, it is according to the other reading: "Will you not come to us, so how will you speak to us?" That is, there is no coming from you, so there is no speaking. Likewise here: they have no partner, so there is no equality and no fear.

The majority read ﴿fear them﴾ with the accusative (*nasb*), with the verbal noun (*masdar*) annexed to its subject; Ibn Abi 'Ubayda read it in the nominative, with the verbal noun annexed to its object. Both are good readings, and there is no impropriety in annexing a verbal noun to its object while the subject is present.

﴿Thus﴾: i.e., like that clarification, ﴿We detail the signs﴾: i.e., We make them clear, because the parable reveals meanings and makes them plain, as it is like a depiction and a shaping of them. Do you not see how He depicted polytheism in a disfigured form? The majority read ﴿We detail﴾ with *nun* (the first-person plural), in agreement with ﴿We have provided﴾. 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Umar, read it with *ya'* of the third person, in consideration of ﴿He has coined﴾, since it is attributed to the third person. Some scholars cited this verse as evidence for the validity of the principle of partnership among created beings, because some depend on others. It is as if He said: what is forbidden and considered abhorrent is the partnership of slaves with their masters; but the partnership of masters with one another is not forbidden nor abhorrent. The transition with *bal* ("but") in His words ﴿But those who wronged follow﴾ came in accordance with what the verse contains, since the meaning is: they have no proof or excuse for their associating others with Allah; rather, it is merely following desire without knowledge, because a person may have a desire while knowing (that it is wrong). ﴿Those who wronged﴾ are the polytheists, who followed their desires, ignorant and wandering aimlessly, not restrained from their desires by knowledge, since they are free of the knowledge that could deter one who follows desire.

﴿So who can guide those whom Allah has led astray?﴾: i.e., no one can guide those whom Allah has led astray; these are among those whom Allah has led astray, so there is no guide for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whom Allah has led astray" means whom Allah has forsaken and not shown kindness to, because He knows that he is one to whom no kindness is extended, from among those whom He could guide, like him. ﴿For them there are no helpers﴾ is evidence that "leading astray" means "forsaking." End of quote, and this is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school).

﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾: i.e., straighten your face toward it, turn to it without looking aside. This is a figure of speech for his turning to the religion, adhering to it, steadfastness in it, and concern for its causes. When a person is concerned with something, he fixes his gaze on it and straightens his face toward it, facing it. The religion is the religion of Islam. The face is mentioned because it gathers the human senses and is the most noble of them. *Hanifan* ("inclining to truth") is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in *aqim* (the imperative "set"), or from "face," or from "religion." Its meaning is: turning away from the altered and abrogated (*mansukha*) religions.

﴿The nature (fitra) of Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, like His words ﴿the coloring of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara 2:138]. It was also said that it is in the accusative by an elided verb whose estimated form is: "hold fast to the nature of Allah." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Adhere to the nature of Allah," or "upon you is the nature of Allah." It was made elided because of the address to the plural, in agreement with His words ﴿turning penitently to Him﴾, where "turning penitently" is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "adhere." The phrase "and establish" and "and do not be" is conjoined to this elided element. End of quote. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿so set your face﴾ is "so set your faces," and it is not specific to the Messenger alone. It seems to be an address to a singular addressee intended to mean the plural, i.e., "so set (yourselves), O addressee," and then the plural is used according to meaning, because a single addressee is not intended. If this is the case, then "turning penitently," "and establish," and "and do not be" carry the sense of the plural. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "or upon you is the nature of Allah," is not permissible, because it involves omitting the word of warning (*ighra'*, the word "upon you," *'alayka*), and it is not permissible to omit it, since the verb has been omitted and "upon you" has been put in its place. If its omission were allowed, it would be a serious imbalance, since it would involve omitting both the substitute and that for which it substitutes.

Al-Fitra (the innate disposition) is said to be the religion of Islam, and "al-nas" (the people) is restricted to the believers. It is also said to be the covenant that God took from the descendants of Adam when He brought them forth from his loins as particles (nasam). The skilled scholars (al-hudhdhaq) preferred that it is the capacity present in the child to reflect upon God's creatures and to infer from them their Originator, so that he believes in Him and follows His laws. However, there may arise external factors that divert him from this, such as his parents making him a Jew or a Christian, and the seduction of the devils of mankind and jinn.

﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾, i.e., there is no alteration of this capacity on the part of the Creator. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd said: there is no alteration of the religion of God, meaning: of the creeds of the religions, since they agree on this. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it is not fitting that this innate disposition be changed or altered. Ibn Abbas said: there is no alteration of God's decree concerning their happiness and misery. It is also said that it is a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, i.e., do not alter that religion. It is also said: ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ in the sense that monotheism is inherent in it, with no change in it, so that even if you asked him, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", he would say, "God." What is reported from Ibn Abbas, that the meaning of ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ is a prohibition against castrating male animals, is strange. The view of one who holds that the meaning of this sentence is a rebuttal of the disbelievers, inserted parenthetically into the speech, as if he were saying: "Establish your face for the religion which has such-and-such attributes, for these disbelievers, and those whom God has created for disbelief..." and ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾, meaning: they do not prosper; that which you were commanded to set your face toward is the religion that is most thorough in uprightness, is also mentioned as an objection. The word al-qayyim (the upright) is an intensive form with the ya', from al-qiyam, in the sense of uprightness. Its pattern is faʻil; its original form is qaywim, like yad; the ya' and waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into ya', and the ya' was assimilated into it. This pattern is specific to hollow-medial roots, and in the sound (non-weak) roots there has come from it only bay'is and sayqal, a proper name for a woman.

(Muniban) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (al-nas), especially if by al-nas is meant the believers; or from the pronoun in "Adhere to the fitra of God"; and this is al-Zamakhshari's estimation; or from the pronoun in "(fa-aqim)", since the intended addressee is the Messenger ﷺ and his community, and it is as if a coordinated element has been omitted, i.e., "establish your face and your community." What points to this is the circumstantial clause (muniban) being in the plural, and in ﴿when you divorce﴾ [al-Talaq: 1] the address is in the plural both there and in what follows. Or it is the predicate of an elided kana, i.e., "be penitent," and what points to it is his later saying (wa-la takunu, "and do not be"). These are all transmitted possibilities. The term of association (ishrak), according to this, is used figuratively, since they became sects in their religion. The apparent meaning is that the mushrikun are everyone who associates partners with God, so the People of the Book and others are included among them. (Min alladhina) is a substitute (badal) for (al-mushrikin). ﴿Who split up their religion﴾, i.e., the religion of Islam, and made it into different religions according to the differences of their desires.

﴿And became sects﴾: each group follows its leader, who was the cause of its misguidance.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that (min alladhina) is disconnected from what precedes it, and its meaning is: "of those who abandon their religion, every party rejoicing in what they have." But he put (farihun) in the nominative as a description of (kull), as in his saying:

"And every friend is not one who humbles his own self"

End of his words. He first estimated (farihin) as genitive, an adjective of hizb, then said: but it was put in the nominative as a description of (kull), because when you say, "From your people is every righteous man (kull rajul salih)," it is permissible for "salih" to be in the genitive as an adjective of "rajul," which is the more common, as in his saying:

"Every abundant eye poured upon him, so they left every garden like a dirham"

and it is permissible to make it nominative as an adjective of (kull), as in his saying:

"And upon him blew every turbulent wind, wild, which has no mind to its reason"

where "hawja'" (wild) is in the nominative as an adjective of "kull."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 30, verses 26–32 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ ﴿It is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and it is easier for Him. To Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you, sharing equally in it, so that you fear them as you fear one another? Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason.﴾ ﴿But those who wronged follow their desires without knowledge. So who can guide those whom Allah has led astray? For them there are no helpers.﴾ ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a people inclining to truth, the nature (fitra) of Allah upon which He created mankind. There is no altering the creation of Allah. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿Turning penitently to Him, and fear Him, and establish prayer, and do not be among the polytheists,﴾ ﴿of those who have divided their religion and become sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has.﴾

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is general, encompassing all of them being under His dominion and subjugation. Al-Hasan said: "qanitun" means standing as witnesses to His oneness, as the poet said:

*"And in everything there is a sign that indicates that He is One."*

Ibn 'Abbas said: "obedient," i.e., in His disposing of them, none of them can resist Him in what He wills to do to them, of life and death, health and sickness. This is obedience of will, not obedience of worship. It was also said: "standing" on the Day of Resurrection, the day when people will stand before the Lord of the worlds. If *qunut* is taken to mean sincerity, as Ibn Jubayr said, or acknowledgment of servitude, or that "devoutly obedient" refers to both angels and believers, then this is because every general statement is subject to specification.

﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: i.e., repetition is easier for Him. *Ahwan* here is not an elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*, the comparative/superlative pattern), because there is no gradation with Allah between the two states of origination and repetition. Therefore Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym interpreted it to mean *hayyin* ("easy"). Likewise it is so in the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud). The pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to Allah. It was also said that *ahwan* is comparative, according to human belief and what observation shows them, that repetition of many things is easier than initial creation, since it does not require the deliberation that initial creation required. Although, for Him, both are equally easy. It was also said that the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to creation, meaning: repetition is easier for creatures, i.e., quicker, because initial creation involves gradual progression from stage to stage until one becomes a human being, whereas repetition does not need these gradual stages of development. Allah simply calls, and they emerge. So it is as if He said: "It is easier for Him," i.e., shorter in duration and less in transition. It was also said that the meaning is: "it is easier for the created being," i.e., one who recreates something after having originated it. This is the custom of created beings, so how do you deny repetition in the case of the Creator? Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In my view, the more apparent is that the pronoun refers to Allah, and this is supported by His words: ﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness﴾, as it came in a wording that contains a seeking of refuge and a drawing of evidence from the created being regarding the Creator, and a comparison with what people know of themselves. The aspect of greatness is pure, in that He is given the highest likeness, which is not connected to Him. How could there be any likeness, when nothing is like Him?" End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why was the complement delayed in His words ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ but placed first in His words ﴿it is easy for Me﴾ [Maryam 19:9]? I say: there, exclusivity was intended, namely His overpowering, so it was said: "it is easy for Me," even though it is difficult in your view, even if it was born between an aged man and a barren woman. Here, however, there is no sense of exclusivity, especially since the matter is based on what they understand, that repetition is easier than initial creation. If the complement had been placed first, the meaning would have changed. End of quote. The basis of his statement is that fronting an element of the sentence indicates exclusivity, and we have discussed this with him and did not accept it in His words: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:5].

﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness﴾: It was said that this is connected to what precedes it, as al-Zajjaj said, namely His words ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾; He has set for you a parable in what is easy or difficult. It was also said that it is connected to what follows it, namely His words ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves.﴾ It was also said: the parable (*mathal*) is the most exalted, highest attribute, which no other shares, namely that He is the One capable who is not unable to do anything, whether origination, repetition, or anything else. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: i.e., the Subduer of everything, ﴿the Wise﴾ whose acts follow the requirement of His wisdom. It is reported from Mujahid that "the highest likeness" is the statement: "There is no god but Allah," and that to Him belongs the attribute of oneness. This is supported by His words ﴿He has coined for you﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and others said: Allah clarified the matter of the idols and the corruption of the belief of those who associate them with Allah, by His coining this parable. Its meaning is: O people, if you have slaves whom you own, you do not make them partners in your wealth and important affairs, nor in anything on the basis of equal standing, nor is it proper for you to fear them lest they inherit your wealth or divide it with you during your lifetime, as some of you do with others. If this is so among you, how can you say that among His slaves and His possessions there are partners in His authority and divinity, and attribute to Him what you do not find fitting for yourselves? This meaning came in the form of a question and affirmation. Al-Suddi said: They used to make their gods inherit, so this was revealed. It was also said: when this was revealed, the people of Mecca said: "That will never be!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then why is it permitted for your Lord?"

The *min* in ﴿from yourselves﴾ indicates the starting point, as if He said: He took a parable and drew it from the nearest thing to you, namely yourselves, and this is not far-fetched. The *min* in ﴿among what﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] indicates partitive meaning. The *min* in ﴿partners﴾ is extra, for emphasizing the interrogative that functions as a negation. It means: none of you is pleased that his slave should share with him in his property, his wife, or what belongs exclusively to him, to the point of being his equal. How, then, would you accept a partner for Allah, while He is the Lord of lords and the Owner of both free people and slaves?

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: There is similarity and dissimilarity between the parable and what it parables. The similarity is known, and the dissimilarity is in several respects. His words ﴿from yourselves﴾ mean from your own offspring, together with the lowliness, deficiency, and weakness of the self, while He compared Himself to you despite His greatness, majesty, and power. His words ﴿among what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] mean your slaves. Ownership is that which precedes transfer by sale and cessation by manumission, and what Allah owns never leaves His ownership. So if your slave may not share with you, though he is like you in every respect and like you in humanity, in the state of slavery, how could a slave share with Allah in every respect, when He is utterly separate from him? His words ﴿in what We have provided for you﴾ mean that the true provider for you is Allah, and the provision is truly from Him. If it is not permitted for a slave to share with you in what is yours in name, how could He have a partner in what truly belongs to Him? End of quote, with some summarizing. The word ﴿partners﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject of the nominal sentence, and ﴿in what We have provided for you﴾ is connected to it, and ﴿for you﴾ is the predicate. ﴿Among what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur 24:33] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), because it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun placed before it, and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and the governing element of it is the governing element of the prepositional phrase, which functions as the predicate, and it is understood after the subject. The *ma* in ﴿what We have provided﴾ refers to the category, and the meaning is: are there partners in what We have provided for you who are of the category that your right hands possess, who belong to you? It is also permitted that ﴿for you﴾ be connected to ﴿partners﴾ and that ﴿of what We have provided for you﴾ be the predicate, as you say: "For Zayd in Medina there is one who hates," so "for Zayd" is connected to "one who hates," which is the subject, and "in Medina" is the predicate. The sentence ﴿so you are in it equal﴾ is in the position of the answer to the interrogative that implies negation, and ﴿in it﴾ is connected to ﴿equal﴾. ﴿You fear them﴾ is a second predicate for ﴿you﴾, and the meaning is: "So you are equal with them in what We have provided for you, you fear them as some of you fear others, O masters." The purpose is to negate partnership, equality, and fear, and the negation does not apply only to the answer and what follows it, as in one of the two readings of: "Will you not come to us and speak to us?" That is, "You do not come to us and speak to us," meaning you come and do not speak. Rather, it is according to the other reading: "Will you not come to us, so how will you speak to us?" That is, there is no coming from you, so there is no speaking. Likewise here: they have no partner, so there is no equality and no fear.

The majority read ﴿fear them﴾ with the accusative (*nasb*), with the verbal noun (*masdar*) annexed to its subject; Ibn Abi 'Ubayda read it in the nominative, with the verbal noun annexed to its object. Both are good readings, and there is no impropriety in annexing a verbal noun to its object while the subject is present.

﴿Thus﴾: i.e., like that clarification, ﴿We detail the signs﴾: i.e., We make them clear, because the parable reveals meanings and makes them plain, as it is like a depiction and a shaping of them. Do you not see how He depicted polytheism in a disfigured form? The majority read ﴿We detail﴾ with *nun* (the first-person plural), in agreement with ﴿We have provided﴾. 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Umar, read it with *ya'* of the third person, in consideration of ﴿He has coined﴾, since it is attributed to the third person. Some scholars cited this verse as evidence for the validity of the principle of partnership among created beings, because some depend on others. It is as if He said: what is forbidden and considered abhorrent is the partnership of slaves with their masters; but the partnership of masters with one another is not forbidden nor abhorrent. The transition with *bal* ("but") in His words ﴿But those who wronged follow﴾ came in accordance with what the verse contains, since the meaning is: they have no proof or excuse for their associating others with Allah; rather, it is merely following desire without knowledge, because a person may have a desire while knowing (that it is wrong). ﴿Those who wronged﴾ are the polytheists, who followed their desires, ignorant and wandering aimlessly, not restrained from their desires by knowledge, since they are free of the knowledge that could deter one who follows desire.

﴿So who can guide those whom Allah has led astray?﴾: i.e., no one can guide those whom Allah has led astray; these are among those whom Allah has led astray, so there is no guide for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whom Allah has led astray" means whom Allah has forsaken and not shown kindness to, because He knows that he is one to whom no kindness is extended, from among those whom He could guide, like him. ﴿For them there are no helpers﴾ is evidence that "leading astray" means "forsaking." End of quote, and this is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school).

﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾: i.e., straighten your face toward it, turn to it without looking aside. This is a figure of speech for his turning to the religion, adhering to it, steadfastness in it, and concern for its causes. When a person is concerned with something, he fixes his gaze on it and straightens his face toward it, facing it. The religion is the religion of Islam. The face is mentioned because it gathers the human senses and is the most noble of them. *Hanifan* ("inclining to truth") is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in *aqim* (the imperative "set"), or from "face," or from "religion." Its meaning is: turning away from the altered and abrogated (*mansukha*) religions.

﴿The nature (fitra) of Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, like His words ﴿the coloring of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara 2:138]. It was also said that it is in the accusative by an elided verb whose estimated form is: "hold fast to the nature of Allah." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Adhere to the nature of Allah," or "upon you is the nature of Allah." It was made elided because of the address to the plural, in agreement with His words ﴿turning penitently to Him﴾, where "turning penitently" is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "adhere." The phrase "and establish" and "and do not be" is conjoined to this elided element. End of quote. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿so set your face﴾ is "so set your faces," and it is not specific to the Messenger alone. It seems to be an address to a singular addressee intended to mean the plural, i.e., "so set (yourselves), O addressee," and then the plural is used according to meaning, because a single addressee is not intended. If this is the case, then "turning penitently," "and establish," and "and do not be" carry the sense of the plural. Al-Zamakhshari's statement, "or upon you is the nature of Allah," is not permissible, because it involves omitting the word of warning (*ighra'*, the word "upon you," *'alayka*), and it is not permissible to omit it, since the verb has been omitted and "upon you" has been put in its place. If its omission were allowed, it would be a serious imbalance, since it would involve omitting both the substitute and that for which it substitutes.

Al-Fitra (the innate disposition) is said to be the religion of Islam, and "al-nas" (the people) is restricted to the believers. It is also said to be the covenant that God took from the descendants of Adam when He brought them forth from his loins as particles (nasam). The skilled scholars (al-hudhdhaq) preferred that it is the capacity present in the child to reflect upon God's creatures and to infer from them their Originator, so that he believes in Him and follows His laws. However, there may arise external factors that divert him from this, such as his parents making him a Jew or a Christian, and the seduction of the devils of mankind and jinn.

﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾, i.e., there is no alteration of this capacity on the part of the Creator. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd said: there is no alteration of the religion of God, meaning: of the creeds of the religions, since they agree on this. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it is not fitting that this innate disposition be changed or altered. Ibn Abbas said: there is no alteration of God's decree concerning their happiness and misery. It is also said that it is a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, i.e., do not alter that religion. It is also said: ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ in the sense that monotheism is inherent in it, with no change in it, so that even if you asked him, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", he would say, "God." What is reported from Ibn Abbas, that the meaning of ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ is a prohibition against castrating male animals, is strange. The view of one who holds that the meaning of this sentence is a rebuttal of the disbelievers, inserted parenthetically into the speech, as if he were saying: "Establish your face for the religion which has such-and-such attributes, for these disbelievers, and those whom God has created for disbelief..." and ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾, meaning: they do not prosper; that which you were commanded to set your face toward is the religion that is most thorough in uprightness, is also mentioned as an objection. The word al-qayyim (the upright) is an intensive form with the ya', from al-qiyam, in the sense of uprightness. Its pattern is faʻil; its original form is qaywim, like yad; the ya' and waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into ya', and the ya' was assimilated into it.
