Then, when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾ ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ ﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, behold, they despair.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen that God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it? Surely in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿So give to the near of kin his due, and to the needy and the wayfarer. That is better for those who seek the Face of God, and it is they who are the successful.﴾ ﴿Whatever you give as usury (ribā) so that it may increase within people's wealth, it does not increase with God. But whatever you give as zakāt (obligatory alms), seeking the Face of God, those are the ones who multiply (their reward).﴾

(Al-Durr) means hardship, whether from poverty, sickness, drought, or something else. (Al-rahma) means deliverance from that hardship.

﴿They called upon their Lord﴾: they devoted their supplication and humble entreaty to Him alone, so that they might be saved from that hardship. They abandoned their idols, knowing that none but Him, exalted is He, removes hardship. So at that time they have turning back (inābah) and submission. But when He delivers them from that hardship, a group of those who had been sincere associates others with Him, and this group is the worshippers of idols. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Something of these expressions also applies to the believers, when relief comes to them after hardship, and they attribute that relief to created beings, or to the cleverness of their opinions, or to something else. In that there is a lack of gratitude to God, and this is called (majāzan) figuratively. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: One who says, "I was saved because of the conjunction of such-and-such star, or because of such-and-such idol," or who ought not to believe he is saved by means of so-and-so when that is apparent, commits hidden shirk (shirk khafī). End of quote.

(Idhā fariq) is the response (jawāb) to the first (idhā adhāqahum), which is a conditional clause. The second idhā is for sudden surprise (lil-mufājaʾa), and its parallel has been mentioned before. Here the word "fariq" (a group) is used because His saying, "When harm touches people," is general, applying to both believer and unbeliever, so only the unbeliever associates others with God. The word "ḍurr" here is unrestricted, whereas at the end of al-ʿAnkabūt the phrase is "idhā hum yushrikūn" [al-ʿAnkabūt: 65], because it refers to a specific group of polytheists, the worshippers of idols, and the harm there is specific, namely what is feared when riding the sea. (Idhā hum) means: the sea-travellers who are idol-worshippers, and what comes before and after it indicates this.

The lām in (li-yakfurū) is the lām of purpose (lām kay), or it is the lām of command for threat (lil-tahdīd). Its parallel has been mentioned at the end of al-ʿAnkabūt.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿fa-tamatta‘ū fa-sawfa ta‘lamūn﴾ with the letter tāʾ in both places. Abū al-ʿĀliya read "fa-yutamatta‘ū" with a yāʾ, in the passive voice, and it is coordinated (maʿṭūf) with (li-yakfurū); and "la-sawfa yaʿlamūn" with a yāʾ, as a threat to them. From Abū al-ʿĀliya also "fa-yatamatta‘ū" with a yāʾ before the tāʾ, also coordinated with (li-yakfurū), meaning: so that their lives may be prolonged in disbelief. From him, and from ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd), "fa-li-yatamatta‘ū" (with a lām of command). Hārūn said that in the Muṣḥaf of ʿAbd Allāh it reads "yatamatta‘ū."

﴿Or have We sent down﴾: "am" here means "bal" (rather), and the hamza is for turning away from the preceding speech. The hamza is also an interrogative for seeking proof, in the form of denial and rebuke. (Sulṭān) means proof, from a book or the like.

﴿So it speaks﴾: that is, it reveals their doctrine and utters their shirk. The attribution of speech is metaphorical, like His saying, "This is Our Book which speaks against you with truth" [al-Jāthiya: 29]. "Fa-huwa yatakallamu" is the answer to the interrogative implied by "am," as if He had said: "Rather, We have sent down to them an authority," that is, a proof bearing witness for you to shirk, so it testifies to the validity of that. If "sulṭān" is understood as "dhū sulṭān" (one possessing authority), that is, a king possessing proof, then the speaking is literal.

﴿When We let people taste mercy﴾: that is, blessing, such as rain, abundance, or health.

﴿But if an evil befalls them﴾: that is, affliction, such as misfortune, constriction, or sickness.

﴿Because of what their hands have sent forth﴾: that is, sins.

His saying, ﴿Indeed God does not change what is in a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. So at the arrival of mercy they rejoice and forget to thank the One who bestowed it upon them, and at the arrival of affliction they despair and lose hope and forget patience, and forget the blessings bestowed upon them before the affliction. (Idhā hum) is the response to (wa-in tuṣibhum), standing in the place of the fāʾ in a nominal clause that is the answer to a conditional.

When He mentioned the granting of mercy, He did not mention its cause, which is increased goodness and bounty. When He mentioned the striking of an evil, He mentioned its cause, which is disobedience, so that its opposite would be made clear. Then He mentioned the matter which whoever contemplates will not despair of the mercy of God, namely that He is the One who extends and the One who restricts. Therefore one should not despair, and should receive what comes from God with patience in affliction and gratitude in blessing, and should refrain from the disobedience that caused the evil to befall him, until the mercy of his Lord returns to him.

The connection of ﴿So give to the near of kin﴾ to what precedes it is this: when He mentioned that He is the One who extends and restricts, and made that a sign for the believer, then He drew attention to kindness toward one who is in need and poverty, because among faith is compassion for God's creatures. So He addressed the one to whom provision has been extended, commanding him to pay God's right from wealth, and to spend it on those nearest to him, such as those performing pilgrimage, and on others: the needy and the wayfarer. Al-Ḥasan said: This is an address to every hearer, regarding the maintenance of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim). And it was said: it is addressed to the Messenger (peace be upon him).

(Dhū al-qurbā) refers to the Banū Hāshim and the Banū al-Muṭṭalib, who are given their rights from the spoils of war (ghanīma) and the fay' (property obtained without battle). Al-Ḥasan said: the right of the needy and the wayfarer is from the alms (ṣadaqa) designated for them.

Abū Ḥanīfa used this verse as evidence for the obligation of maintenance (nafaqa) for close relatives (maḥārim) when they are needy and unable to earn. God has established a right for the near of kin, and for the needy and the wayfarer, their respective rights.

The sūrah is Meccan, so the apparent meaning is that the right is not zakāt; rather it becomes a right by way of kindness and consolation. For the sake of emphasis on the near of kin, he was placed before the needy and the wayfarer, because his kindness is both charity and kinship ties.

﴿That﴾: that is, the giving, ﴿is better﴾: that is, their reward will be multiplied in the Hereafter, and their wealth will grow in this world, for the sake of the Face of God, that is, seeking nearness to the pleasure of God, which does not harm them.

Then He mentioned those who dispose of their wealth in a way other than the approved manner, saying: ﴿Whatever you give﴾ — the eaters of usury (ribā) — so that it may increase and grow in wealth, it does not grow with God, and it is not blessed, as in His saying: ﴿God destroys usury and makes charity grow﴾ [al-Baqara: 276].

Al-Suddī said: it was revealed concerning the usury of Thaqīf, who practised usury, and Quraysh practised it upon them. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, and Ṭāwūs said: this verse was revealed concerning gifts given for reward (hibāt li-l-thawāb). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what is similar to these, of what is done for recompense, like the gift in exchange, and other things, even though there is no sin in it, there is no reward in it and no increase with God. Ibn ʿAbbās also said, and al-Nakhaʿī: it was revealed concerning people who give to their relatives and brothers in order to benefit them and enrich them, and to show favour to them, and so that they may increase their wealth by way of benefit through it; that benefit is for them. Al-Shaʿbī said something similar to this, namely: whatever a person serves another with, he benefits from it, and that benefit is for them. Al-Shaʿbī also said something similar to this, namely: that it does not increase with God. The apparent meaning is the first view, which is the prohibition of usury.

The majority read the first ﴿wa-mā ātaytum﴾ with a madda on the hamza, meaning "and what you have given"; Ibn Kathīr read it with a short vowel (qaṣr), meaning "and what you have come with." The majority read (li-yarbū) with a yāʾ and the verb attributed to usury (ribā); Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Abū Rajāʾ, al-Shaʿbī, Nāfiʿ, and Abū Ḥaywa read it with a tāʾ, with damma, and the verb attributed to them (the givers). Abū Mālik read "li-yurbūhā," with a feminine pronoun.

The one who is "al-muḍʿaf" (the multiplier) is one who has multiples (aḍʿāf) in reward. Al-Farrāʾ said: they are the people of multiplication, just as you say "huwa musammin" (he is one who has fat [animals]), meaning: the owner of fat camels, and "muʿaṭṭash" (one who has thirsty camels). Ubayy read "al-muḍʿafūn" with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, as a passive participle (ism mafʿūl). Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿fa-ulā'ika hum al-muḍʿifūn﴾ is a fine shift (iltifāt), as if He said to His angels and the elect of His creation: "Those who seek the Face of God with their charities, they are the multipliers," and the meaning is "the multipliers thereby" (bihi), by the indication of "ulā'ika hum al-muḍʿifūn." The omission is due to the evidence in the speech for it, and this interpretation is easier to grasp, while the first is richer in benefit. End of quote. He needed to supply what he supplied, because the conditional noun (ism al-shart) is not an adverb of time, so there must be in the response a pronoun referring back to it, through which the connection is completed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 30, verse 40–45:

﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will bring you to life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that? Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, so that He may let them taste part of what they have done, that they might return.﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before; most of them were polytheists."﴾ ﴿So direct your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be turned back. That Day they will be divided.﴾ ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief; and whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare [a resting place].﴾ ﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds from His bounty. Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers.﴾

The Exalted repeated His address to the disbelievers concerning their idols. He mentioned His acts in which no partner can be claimed for Him: creating, providing, causing death, and giving life. Then He asked a question in the form of affirmation for them and rebuke, and then He declared Himself far above their statement. The phrase ﴿Allah is He who created you﴾ is a subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible that (alladhi khalaqakum) be a qualifier of the subject, and the predicate be: (hal min shurakaikum)." His saying: (min dhalikum) is what linked the sentence to the subject, because its meaning is: from His acts. End of quote. What the grammarians have stated is that the demonstrative pronoun serves as a link when it refers to the subject. As for (dhalikum) here, it is not a reference to the subject, but it resembles what al-Farra' permitted of linking by meaning, and people disagreed with him, concerning His saying: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]. He said: the estimate is: "yatarabbasna azwajahum" (let them wait, their husbands), so he estimated the pronoun with a noun added to the pronoun of (alladhina), and thereby the link was achieved. Likewise, al-Zamakhshari estimated (min dhalikum) as "min af'alihi" (from His acts), which is added to the pronoun returning to the subject. Al-Zamakhshari also said: "Is there any of your partners whom you have taken as equals to Him, of the idols and others, who does ever (qatt) any of those acts, so that what you claimed would be valid?" He used (qatt) in a place other than its proper place, because it is an adverb of past time, and here he made it governed by (yaf'alu). Al-Zamakhshari also said: "The (min) in the first and second [occurrences] are each indicating the future, as an emphasis on the incapacity of their partners and the ignorance of their worshippers. So the first (min) is for partitive [meaning], and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of the subject; (man yaf'alu) is the subject, and the second (min) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier from (shay'), because it is an indefinite qualifier placed before it, so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative; and the third (min) is superfluous because the interrogation whose meaning is negation extends to the speech; the estimate is: 'who does anything of that,' i.e., of those acts."

The majority read (yushrikuna) with the ya' of the third person; al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read it with the ta' of address. The apparent meaning is the apparent land and sea. Al-Hasan said: The appearance of corruption in them is by the removal of blessings, the descent of calamities, the occurrence of trials, and the domination of a disbelieving enemy; these three exist on land and sea. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿The corruption on land﴾ is highway robbers who block the way. Mujahid said: (on land) is by one of the children of Adam killing his brother, and (on sea) is by seizing ships by force. He also said: "land" means the countries far from the sea, and "sea" means the coasts and islands that are on the bank of the sea and rivers. Qatadah said: "land" means the deserts, the places of tribes, and the people of the open country and the cultivated lands, and "sea" means the cities, plural of bahrah; from this is: "The people of this little sea (buhayrah) have indeed agreed to crown him," meaning the saying of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah about 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. This is supported by the reading of 'Ikrimah: "wal-buhur" in the plural, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Corruption had appeared on land and sea at the time of the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and injustice had covered the earth, so Allah made the religion manifest through him, removed corruption, and extinguished it. Al-Nahhas said: In it there are two opinions: one of them: drought appeared on land in the deserts, and he read "wal-bahr" [i.e., the cities of the sea], like: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning scarcity of vegetation appeared, and prices rose. The second: sins appeared, such as highway robbery and injustice; this is corruption in the true sense, and the first is metaphorical. It was said: when rain is scarce, diving decreases, the fisherman is distressed, and the creatures of the sea become blind. Ibn 'Abbas said: when it rains, the shells in the sea open, and whatever falls into them from the sky becomes pearls.

﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾: that is, because of their disobediences and sins.

﴿so that He may let them taste﴾: that is, He corrupted the causes of their worldly life and destroyed them, so that He may let them taste the consequence of some of their deeds in this world, before He punishes them for all of them in the Hereafter.

﴿that they might return﴾ from what they are in. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: (by what they earned) is the recompense for what they earned, and the (ba') may be connected to (appeared), meaning: by their earning of disobediences in land and sea, which is the very corruption that appeared. The readers al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Abu Haywah, Sallam, Sahl, Rawh, Ibn Hassan, and Qunbul via Ibn Mujahid, Ibn al-Sabbah, Abu al-Fadl al-Wasiti from him, and Mahbub from Abu 'Amr read: "linudhiqahum" with the nun; the majority with the ya'. Then He commanded them to travel through the earth so that they might observe how He destroyed the nations because of their disobediences and their association of partners, and that is an admonition to Quraysh and a command to them to take lesson from those who preceded from the nations: the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and others.

﴿most of them were polytheists﴾: He destroyed them all because of polytheism, and some because of sins, since He destroys through sins as He destroys through polytheism, like the People of the Sabbath. Or He destroyed them all, both the polytheist and the believer, like His saying: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike those among you who wronged in particular﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. And He destroyed them all, while they were disbelievers; so most of them were polytheists and some of them were deniers of the Creator (mu'attil). When He mentioned His favor He said: ﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you﴾, so He mentioned existence, then continuance by means of provision. When He mentioned their abandonment in transgression, by means of continuance through the manifestation of corruption, then by means of existence through destruction.

﴿before there comes a Day﴾: the Day of Resurrection, and in it is a warning that encompasses people. ﴿that cannot be turned back from Allah﴾: al-Marad is the verbal noun of radda, and (min Allah) may be connected to "ya'ti" (comes), meaning: before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back so that it does not come, because of His saying: ﴿so they cannot avert it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 40]. It may also be connected to an omitted element indicated by (maradd), meaning: it cannot be turned back by Him after it has come, nor is there any turning back of it on His part. (That day) means: the day when that Day comes. (They will be divided) means they will separate: a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze. It is said: "tasaddaʿa al-qawm" when they dispersed, and from it is al-suda' (headache), because it splits the parts of the head. The poet said:

"We were like the two companions of Judhaymah for a period of time, until it was said they would never part."

Then He mentioned the two conditions of those who separate: ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾: that is, the requital of his disbelief. He expressed the state of the disbeliever with (upon him), which indicates effort and hardship, and the state of the believer with His saying: ﴿for themselves﴾ with the lam which is the lam of ownership. (Yamhadun) means they prepare the ground, and it is a metaphor from spreading out a bed, and an expression of their doing in the world what will lead to what delights their eyes and gladdens their souls in Paradise. Mujahid said: it is preparing the grave. Al-Zamakhshari said: The fronting of the adverbial phrase in both places indicates that the harm of disbelief returns only upon the disbeliever and does not go beyond him, while the benefit of faith and righteous deeds returns to the believer and does not exceed him. End of quote. This is in line with his claim that fronting the object and what is similar to it indicates exclusivity; according to our view it indicates emphasis. As for what he claims of exclusivity, it is understood from many verses of the Qur'an, among them: ﴿And every soul earns only against itself, and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. As for the lam in (liyajziya), al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to (yamhadun), as a reason for it. The repetition of (those who believed and did righteous deeds), and leaving the pronoun for the explicit noun, is to indicate that in his view none succeeds with Him except the believing righteous. His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾ is an affirmation after an affirmation, by way of the converse and the contrapositive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: (liyajziya) is connected to (yassaddaʿun), and it may be connected to an omitted element whose estimate is "that is for He to reward," and the demonstrative refers to what was established in His saying (whoever disbelieves) and (whoever does righteousness). End of quote. On these two estimates the counterpart of (those who believed and did righteous deeds) is omitted, its estimate being: as if He said: "and the disbelievers, after that, are for Him"; and the omission of this counterpart is indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾. The meaning of negating love here is that the signs of His mercy do not appear upon them, and He does not accept disbelief as a religion for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: (min fadlihi) means with what He bestows upon them beyond fulfilling the due reward; this resembles a metonymy, because bounty follows reward, so it occurs only after what follows it has occurred; or He meant from His giving, which is His reward, because bounties and superfluities are the gifts in the Arabic usage.

The second: sins appeared, such as highway robbery and injustice; this is corruption in the true sense, and the first is metaphorical. It was said: when rain is scarce, diving decreases, the fisherman is distressed, and the creatures of the sea become blind. Ibn 'Abbas said: when it rains, the shells in the sea open, and whatever falls into them from the sky becomes pearls.

﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾: that is, because of their disobediences and sins.

﴿so that He may let them taste﴾: that is, He corrupted the causes of their worldly life and destroyed them, so that He may let them taste the consequence of some of their deeds in this world, before He punishes them for all of them in the Hereafter.

﴿that they might return﴾ from what they are in. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: (by what they earned) is the recompense for what they earned, and the (ba') may be connected to (appeared), meaning: by their earning of disobediences in land and sea, which is the very corruption that appeared. The readers al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Abu Haywah, Sallam, Sahl, Rawh, Ibn Hassan, and Qunbul via Ibn Mujahid, Ibn al-Sabbah, Abu al-Fadl al-Wasiti from him, and Mahbub from Abu 'Amr read: "linudhiqahum" with the nun; the majority with the ya'. Then He commanded them to travel through the earth so that they might observe how He destroyed the nations because of their disobediences and their association of partners, and that is an admonition to Quraysh and a command to them to take lesson from those who preceded from the nations: the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and others.

﴿most of them were polytheists﴾: He destroyed them all because of polytheism, and some because of sins, since He destroys through sins as He destroys through polytheism, like the People of the Sabbath. Or He destroyed them all, both the polytheist and the believer, like His saying: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike those among you who wronged in particular﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. And He destroyed them all, while they were disbelievers; so most of them were polytheists and some of them were deniers of the Creator (mu'attil). When He mentioned His favor He said: ﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you﴾, so He mentioned existence, then continuance by means of provision. When He mentioned their abandonment in transgression, by means of continuance through the manifestation of corruption, then by means of existence through destruction.

﴿before there comes a Day﴾: the Day of Resurrection, and in it is a warning that encompasses people. ﴿that cannot be turned back from Allah﴾: al-Marad is the verbal noun of radda, and (min Allah) may be connected to "ya'ti" (comes), meaning: before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back so that it does not come, because of His saying: ﴿so they cannot avert it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 40]. It may also be connected to an omitted element indicated by (maradd), meaning: it cannot be turned back by Him after it has come, nor is there any turning back of it on His part. (That day) means: the day when that Day comes. (They will be divided) means they will separate: a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze. It is said: "tasaddaʿa al-qawm" when they dispersed, and from it is al-suda' (headache), because it splits the parts of the head. The poet said:

"We were like the two companions of Judhaymah for a period of time, until it was said they would never part."

Then He mentioned the two conditions of those who separate: ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾: that is, the requital of his disbelief. He expressed the state of the disbeliever with (upon him), which indicates effort and hardship, and the state of the believer with His saying: ﴿for themselves﴾ with the lam which is the lam of ownership. (Yamhadun) means they prepare the ground, and it is a metaphor from spreading out a bed, and an expression of their doing in the world what will lead to what delights their eyes and gladdens their souls in Paradise. Mujahid said: it is preparing the grave. Al-Zamakhshari said: The fronting of the adverbial phrase in both places indicates that the harm of disbelief returns only upon the disbeliever and does not go beyond him, while the benefit of faith and righteous deeds returns to the believer and does not exceed him. End of quote. This is in line with his claim that fronting the object and what is similar to it indicates exclusivity; according to our view it indicates emphasis. As for what he claims of exclusivity, it is understood from many verses of the Qur'an, among them: ﴿And every soul earns only against itself, and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. As for the lam in (liyajziya), al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to (yamhadun), as a reason for it. The repetition of (those who believed and did righteous deeds), and leaving the pronoun for the explicit noun, is to indicate that in his view none succeeds with Him except the believing righteous. His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾ is an affirmation after an affirmation, by way of the converse and the contrapositive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: (liyajziya) is connected to (yassaddaʿun), and it may be connected to an omitted element whose estimate is "that is for He to reward," and the demonstrative refers to what was established in His saying (whoever disbelieves) and (whoever does righteousness). End of quote. On these two estimates the counterpart of (those who believed and did righteous deeds) is omitted, its estimate being: as if He said: "and the disbelievers, after that, are for Him"; and the omission of this counterpart is indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾. The meaning of negating love here is that the signs of His mercy do not appear upon them, and He does not accept disbelief as a religion for them. Al-Zamakhshari said: (min fadlihi) means with what He bestows upon them beyond fulfilling the due reward; this resembles a metonymy, because bounty follows reward, so it occurs only after what follows it has occurred; or He meant from His giving, which is His reward, because bounties and superfluities are the gifts in the Arabic usage.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 30, verse 40–45:

﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will bring you to life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that? Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, so that He may let them taste part of what they have done, that they might return.﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before; most of them were polytheists."﴾ ﴿So direct your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be turned back. That Day they will be divided.﴾ ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief; and whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare [a resting place].﴾ ﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds from His bounty. Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers.﴾

The Exalted repeated His address to the disbelievers concerning their idols. He mentioned His acts in which no partner can be claimed for Him: creating, providing, causing death, and giving life. Then He asked a question in the form of affirmation for them and rebuke, and then He declared Himself far above their statement. The phrase ﴿Allah is He who created you﴾ is a subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible that (alladhi khalaqakum) be a qualifier of the subject, and the predicate be: (hal min shurakaikum)." His saying: (min dhalikum) is what linked the sentence to the subject, because its meaning is: from His acts. End of quote. What the grammarians have stated is that the demonstrative pronoun serves as a link when it refers to the subject. As for (dhalikum) here, it is not a reference to the subject, but it resembles what al-Farra' permitted of linking by meaning, and people disagreed with him, concerning His saying: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]. He said: the estimate is: "yatarabbasna azwajahum" (let them wait, their husbands), so he estimated the pronoun with a noun added to the pronoun of (alladhina), and thereby the link was achieved. Likewise, al-Zamakhshari estimated (min dhalikum) as "min af'alihi" (from His acts), which is added to the pronoun returning to the subject. Al-Zamakhshari also said: "Is there any of your partners whom you have taken as equals to Him, of the idols and others, who does ever (qatt) any of those acts, so that what you claimed would be valid?" He used (qatt) in a place other than its proper place, because it is an adverb of past time, and here he made it governed by (yaf'alu). Al-Zamakhshari also said: "The (min) in the first and second [occurrences] are each indicating the future, as an emphasis on the incapacity of their partners and the ignorance of their worshippers. So the first (min) is for partitive [meaning], and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of the subject; (man yaf'alu) is the subject, and the second (min) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier from (shay'), because it is an indefinite qualifier placed before it, so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative; and the third (min) is superfluous because the interrogation whose meaning is negation extends to the speech; the estimate is: 'who does anything of that,' i.e., of those acts."

The majority read (yushrikuna) with the ya' of the third person; al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read it with the ta' of address. The apparent meaning is the apparent land and sea. Al-Hasan said: The appearance of corruption in them is by the removal of blessings, the descent of calamities, the occurrence of trials, and the domination of a disbelieving enemy; these three exist on land and sea. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿The corruption on land﴾ is highway robbers who block the way. Mujahid said: (on land) is by one of the children of Adam killing his brother, and (on sea) is by seizing ships by force. He also said: "land" means the countries far from the sea, and "sea" means the coasts and islands that are on the bank of the sea and rivers. Qatadah said: "land" means the deserts, the places of tribes, and the people of the open country and the cultivated lands, and "sea" means the cities, plural of bahrah; from this is: "The people of this little sea (buhayrah) have indeed agreed to crown him," meaning the saying of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah about 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. This is supported by the reading of 'Ikrimah: "wal-buhur" in the plural, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Corruption had appeared on land and sea at the time of the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and injustice had covered the earth, so Allah made the religion manifest through him, removed corruption, and extinguished it. Al-Nahhas said: In it there are two opinions: one of them: drought appeared on land in the deserts, and he read "wal-bahr" [i.e., the cities of the sea], like: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning scarcity of vegetation appeared, and prices rose. The second: sins appeared, such as highway robbery and injustice; this is corruption in the true sense, and the first is metaphorical. [p. 178] When Allah Most High mentioned the appearance of corruption and destruction caused by shirk, He mentioned the appearance of righteousness. The Generous does not mention a reward for His benevolence, but He does mention a cause for His punishment, so that it is not imagined to be injustice. Among the signs of His power, He mentioned the sending of winds as "bearers of good tidings" (mubashshirat) of rain, because they precede it. The "bearers of good tidings" are the winds of mercy: the south wind, the north wind and the east wind. As for the dabur (the west wind), it is the wind of punishment. Its good tidings are not restricted to rain alone; it also brings good tidings through ships and their sailing to their owners' destinations. It seems that He began with something general, which is the giving of good tidings. Al-A'mash read *al-rih* (the wind) in the singular, meaning the plural, and for this reason he read *mubashshirat* (in the plural). Then He mentioned, among the greatest of its good tidings, the tasting of mercy, which is the descent of rain. It is followed by the attainment of fertility, the wind that blows with it, the removal of foulness from the air, the winnowing of grains, and other things.

﴿Wa-li-yudhiqakum﴾ ("and that He may let you taste") is coordinated (ʿatf) with the sense of *mubashshirat* (bearers of good tidings), so the governing element is *an yursil* (that He sends). This is coordination based on an assumed meaning (ʿatf ʿala al-tawahhum), as if it had been said: "to give you good tidings." The circumstantial clause (hal) and the descriptive clause (sifah) may both come, and each carries the sense of causation. You say: "Insult Zayd, the wicked one, and honour Zayd, the learned one," meaning "because of his wickedness" and "because of his learning." It has also been said that what the lam governs is omitted, meaning: "But We sent them." It has also been said that the waw in *wa-li-yudhiqakum* is superfluous. *Bi-amrih* ("by His command") means by the command of Allah. The point is that since the act of running is attributed to the ships, He informs us that it is by His command, may He be exalted. *Min fadlih* ("of His bounty") refers to what the wind makes available to you for trade at sea and to the spoils of the people of shirk.

Then He made clear to His Messenger, by setting before him the example of those prophets whom He had sent. Since Allah Most High had explained the two foundations, the origin (*al-mabda*) and the return (*al-maʿad*), He now explained the third foundation, which is prophethood. In the speech there is an omission, whose sense is: "Some believed in it and some denied it," followed by *fa-intaqamna min alladhina ajramu* ("so We took vengeance upon those who committed crime").

In His saying *wa-kana haqqan ʿalayna nasr al-muʾminin* ("and it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers") there is good news to the Messenger and to his community of victory and triumph, since He informed that those who believed like those believers would be helped. The word *haqqan* ("incumbent") carries emphasis on necessity, an honouring of the believers, and a demonstration of the excellence of prior faith, in that He made them deserving of help and victory. The apparent view is that *haqqan* is the predicate of *kana* and *nasr al-muʾminin* is its subject. It was placed later because what is connected to it forms the closing (*fasilah*) for the sake of emphasis on the recompense, since that is the focus of the benefit. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Some reciters paused on *haqqan* and took it as part of the preceding speech, then began a new sentence with *ʿalayna nasr al-muʾminin*. This is a weak view, because he did not consider the rank of what it presents within the structure of the verse. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be paused upon *haqqan*, and its meaning is: "And the taking of vengeance upon them was just," then one begins with *ʿalayna nasr al-muʾminin*. End of quotation. In pausing on *wa-kana haqqan*, there is a clarification that the vengeance was not an injustice, but justice, because their continued existence yielded nothing except an increase in sin and the begetting of the wicked disbeliever. Their non-existence was therefore better than their corrupt existence.

*Allahu alladhi yursil al-riyah* ("It is Allah who sends the winds") is connected to His saying *wa-min ayatihi an yursil al-riyah mubashshirat* ("And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good tidings"). The sentence between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ). It came to comfort the Messenger, to console him, to promise him victory, and to warn the people of disbelief. In the sending of the winds there is both power and wisdom. As for power, the subtle air that precedes the lightning is such that it uproots trees and demolishes buildings, yet it does not do this by its own essence, but by a free agent. As for wisdom, it lies in what the very blowing of the wind leads to: stirring up clouds, bringing water out of them, the growth of crops, the milking of the udder, and its being specific to some people and not others. This is a profound wisdom, well known through the will (*al-mashiʾah*), the stirring (*al-ithārah*), its movement and its direction. *Al-basṭ* (spreading) is its scattering across the horizons, and *al-kisaf* are pieces. The discussion of His saying *fa-tara al-wadq yakhruju min khilalih* ("then you see the rain coming out from within it") has already been given, and the disagreement concerning *kisafan* and its state (ḥal) from the viewpoint of the reciters has been mentioned. The pronoun in *min khilalih* ("from within it") apparently refers to the cloud, since it is the subject being spoken about. The pronoun is masculine because *al-sahab* (cloud) is a collective noun which may be treated as masculine or feminine. It has been said that it may also refer to *kisafan* in the reading of one who pronounces the ʿayn with a sukun. By *al-sama'* (the sky) is meant the height of the sky, as in His saying: "and its branch is in the sky" [Ibrahim: 24].

*Fa-idha asaba bihi man yasha'* ("then when He strikes with it whom He wills") means: when He causes it to strike the land of whom He wills, their joy comes upon them suddenly, and their delight is not delayed. Al-Akhfash said: *min qablih* is an emphasis for His saying *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* ("before it was sent down upon them").

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it conveys the information of the swiftness with which human hearts turn from despair (*ibласs*) to joy, because His saying *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* may imply a stretch of time, meaning: "long before it was sent down," such as days or the like. So the phrase *min qabli* comes to mean that this is connected to the rain, and thus it is a restricted emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: It carries the meaning of emphasis, and it indicates that their period of expectation for the rain had lengthened and grown distant, so their despair became firm and their despair persisted. Thus the joy is in proportion to their concern for it. End of quotation. However, what Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari mention as the benefit of emphasis in *min qablih* does not appear evident. Rather, its mention is merely for simple emphasis, and it only removes the possibility of metaphor. Qutrub said: The estimate is: "And even if they were, before the descent, before the rain." End of quotation. The phrase "before the sending down of the rain" becomes "before the rain," and this construction is not permissible in eloquent speech, let alone in the Qur'an. It has also been said: the estimate is "before the sending down of the rain": "before they planted," and the rain indicates the crops, because the crops come out through the rain. This is indicated by His saying *fa-ra'awhu musfarran* ("then they see it turned yellow"), meaning the crops. End of quotation. This does not hold, because *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* is connected to *la-mublisin* ("in despair"). It is not possible that *min qabli* (before) with the crops would be connected to *mublisin*, because two prepositions cannot govern a single governing word unless it is through a conjunction (*ʿatf*) or in the manner of apposition (*badal*). The structure here is not with a conjunction, and apposition is not valid, since the sending down of rain is not the crops, nor are the crops a part of it. Some have imagined here a *badal al-ishtimal* (apposition of inclusion) with forced interpretation, either because the sending down includes the crops, in the sense that the crops arise from the sending down, so that the sending down is as if it contained them. This is according to the view of those who say that the first contains the second. Al-Mubarrad said: The second is the clouds, and this also needs a conjunction so that the two prepositions can be connected to *mublisin*. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "before the sending" (*min qabli al-irsal*). Al-Kirmani said: "before the joy" (*min qabli al-istibshar*), because it paired it with despair, and because He conferred the joy upon them. End of quotation. The statement of Ibn ʿIsa and that of al-Kirmani require a conjunction. If one claims that the pronoun in *min qablih* refers to something other than the sending down of rain, the conjunction would have to be omitted. That is possible, but the omission of the conjunction on its own is disputed: is it analogous (*yanqasu*) or not? The omission of the conjunction with clauses is permissible, but its omission alone is the matter of dispute.

The two Ḥaramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafiʿ... in the Meccan and Medinan readings), Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr read *ila athar* in the singular. The rest of the seven read it in the plural. Salam read it with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the thaʾ. Al-Jahdari, Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ and Abu Hayawa read *tuhyi* with a taʾ, for the feminine, and the pronoun refers to the mercy. The author of al-Lawami says: He made the *athar* feminine because it is connected to the mercy by annexation (*idafah*), so it acquired the feminine from it. Such a thing is not permitted unless the annexed noun has the sense of the noun annexed to, or is from its cause. If it is foreign, it is not permitted in any way. End of quotation. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *nuhyi*, with the plural of majesty (*nun al-ʿaẓamah*). The majority read *yuhyi* with the third person masculine (ya' al-ghaybah), and the pronoun refers to Allah. The plural reading *athar* supports this. It has also been said that it refers to *athar* in the reading of the one who used the singular. Ibn Jinni said: *kayfa yuhyi* ("how He gives life") is a clause in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (ḥal), on the basis of meaning, as if he said: "giving life." This requires consideration. *Inna dhalika* ("indeed that") refers to the One capable of giving life to the earth after its death; He is the One who gives life to people after their death. This informs by way of analogy regarding resurrection, and resurrection is among the things over which Allah Most High has power.

*Wa-la-in arsalna riḥan* ("and if We send a wind") informs us of the state of the human being's fluctuation: that after rejoicing at the rain, Allah sends a wind and the vegetation turns yellow with it. *La-zallu yakfurun* ("they would certainly continue to disbelieve") means they would deny out of distress. The wind that turns vegetation yellow is *ṣirr ḥarur* (a scorching cold wind), and both of these cause the plants to become dry stubble (*hashim*). *Al-ḥarur* is the side of the north wind when it storms. The pronoun in *fa-ra'awhu* refers to what is understood from the context, which is the vegetation. It has been said that it refers to the *athar*, because the mercy is the rain and its trace is the vegetation. As for the one who read *athar* in the plural, he returns the pronoun to the traces of mercy, which is the vegetation. The word for vegetation applies to the few and the many, because it is a verbal noun used as a name for what grows. Ibn ʿIsa said: The pronoun in *fa-ra'awhu* refers to the clouds, because when the clouds turn yellow they do not rain. It has also been said that it refers to the wind, but these two views are weak. This is a weak view, because he did not consider the rank of what it presents within the structure of the verse. The discussion of His saying *fa-tara al-wadq yakhruju min khilalih* ("then you see the rain coming out from within it") has already been given, and the disagreement concerning *kisafan* and its state (ḥal) from the viewpoint of the reciters has been mentioned. The pronoun in *min khilalih* ("from within it") apparently refers to the cloud, since it is the subject being spoken about. The pronoun is masculine because *al-sahab* (cloud) is a collective noun which may be treated as masculine or feminine. It has been said that it may also refer to *kisafan* in the reading of one who pronounces the ʿayn with a sukun. By *al-sama'* (the sky) is meant the height of the sky, as in His saying: "and its branch is in the sky" [Ibrahim: 24].

*Fa-idha asaba bihi man yasha'* ("then when He strikes with it whom He wills") means: when He causes it to strike the land of whom He wills, their joy comes upon them suddenly, and their delight is not delayed. Al-Akhfash said: *min qablih* is an emphasis for His saying *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* ("before it was sent down upon them").

So the phrase *min qabli* comes to mean that this is connected to the rain, and thus it is a restricted emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: It carries the meaning of emphasis, and it indicates that their period of expectation for the rain had lengthened and grown distant, so their despair became firm and their despair persisted. Thus the joy is in proportion to their concern for it. End of quotation. However, what Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari mention as the benefit of emphasis in *min qablih* does not appear evident. Rather, its mention is merely for simple emphasis, and it only removes the possibility of metaphor. Qutrub said: The estimate is: "And even if they were, before the descent, before the rain." End of quotation. The phrase "before the sending down of the rain" becomes "before the rain," and this construction is not permissible in eloquent speech, let alone in the Qur'an. It has also been said: the estimate is "before the sending down of the rain": "before they planted," and the rain indicates the crops, because the crops come out through the rain. This is indicated by His saying *fa-ra'awhu musfarran* ("then they see it turned yellow"), meaning the crops. End of quotation. This does not hold, because *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* is connected to *la-mublisin* ("in despair"). The omission of the conjunction with clauses is permissible, but its omission alone is the matter of dispute.

It has been said that it refers to the *athar*, because the mercy is the rain and its trace is the vegetation. As for the one who read *athar* in the plural, he returns the pronoun to the traces of mercy, which is the vegetation. *Fa-idha asaba bihi man yasha'* ("then when He strikes with it whom He wills") means: when He causes it to strike the land of whom He wills, their joy comes upon them suddenly, and their delight is not delayed. Al-Akhfash said: *min qablih* is an emphasis for His saying *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* ("before it was sent down upon them").

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it conveys the information of the swiftness with which human hearts turn from despair (*ibласs*) to joy, because His saying *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* may imply a stretch of time, meaning: "long before it was sent down," such as days or the like. So the phrase *min qabli* comes to mean that this is connected to the rain, and thus it is a restricted emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: It carries the meaning of emphasis, and it indicates that their period of expectation for the rain had lengthened and grown distant, so their despair became firm and their despair persisted. Thus the joy is in proportion to their concern for it. End of quotation. However, what Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari mention as the benefit of emphasis in *min qablih* does not appear evident. Rather, its mention is merely for simple emphasis, and it only removes the possibility of metaphor. Qutrub said: The estimate is: "And even if they were, before the descent, before the rain." End of quotation. The phrase "before the sending down of the rain" becomes "before the rain," and this construction is not permissible in eloquent speech, let alone in the Qur'an. It has also been said: the estimate is "before the sending down of the rain": "before they planted," and the rain indicates the crops, because the crops come out through the rain. This is indicated by His saying *fa-ra'awhu musfarran* ("then they see it turned yellow"), meaning the crops. End of quotation. This does not hold, because *min qabli an yunazzala ʿalayhim* is connected to *la-mublisin* ("in despair"). It is not possible that *min qabli* (before) with the crops would be connected to *mublisin*, because two prepositions cannot govern a single governing word unless it is through a conjunction (*ʿatf*) or in the manner of apposition (*badal*). The structure here is not with a conjunction, and apposition is not valid, since the sending down of rain is not the crops, nor are the crops a part of it. Some have imagined here a *badal al-ishtimal* (apposition of inclusion) with forced interpretation, either because the sending down includes the crops, in the sense that the crops arise from the sending down, so that the sending down is as if it contained them. This is according to the view of those who say that the first contains the second. Al-Mubarrad said: The second is the clouds, and this also needs a conjunction so that the two prepositions can be connected to *mublisin*. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "before the sending" (*min qabli al-irsal*). Al-Kirmani said: "before the joy" (*min qabli al-istibshar*), because it paired it with despair, and because He conferred the joy upon them. End of quotation. The statement of Ibn ʿIsa and that of al-Kirmani require a conjunction. If one claims that the pronoun in *min qablih* refers to something other than the sending down of rain, the conjunction would have to be omitted. That is possible, but the omission of the conjunction on its own is disputed: is it analogous (*yanqasu*) or not? The omission of the conjunction with clauses is permissible, but its omission alone is the matter of dispute.

The two Ḥaramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafiʿ... in the Meccan and Medinan readings), Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr read *ila athar* in the singular. The rest of the seven read it in the plural. Salam read it with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the thaʾ. Al-Jahdari, Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ and Abu Hayawa read *tuhyi* with a taʾ, for the feminine, and the pronoun refers to the mercy. The author of al-Lawami says: He made the *athar* feminine because it is connected to the mercy by annexation (*idafah*), so it acquired the feminine from it. Such a thing is not permitted unless the annexed noun has the sense of the noun annexed to, or is from its cause. If it is foreign, it is not permitted in any way. End of quotation. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *nuhyi*, with the plural of majesty (*nun al-ʿaẓamah*). The majority read *yuhyi* with the third person masculine (ya' al-ghaybah), and the pronoun refers to Allah. The plural reading *athar* supports this. It has also been said that it refers to *athar* in the reading of the one who used the singular. Ibn Jinni said: *kayfa yuhyi* ("how He gives life") is a clause in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (ḥal), on the basis of meaning, as if he said: "giving life." This requires consideration. *Inna dhalika* ("indeed that") refers to the One capable of giving life to the earth after its death; He is the One who gives life to people after their death. This informs by way of analogy regarding resurrection, and resurrection is among the things over which Allah Most High has power.

*Wa-la-in arsalna riḥan* ("and if We send a wind") informs us of the state of the human being's fluctuation: that after rejoicing at the rain, Allah sends a wind and the vegetation turns yellow with it. *La-zallu yakfurun* ("they would certainly continue to disbelieve") means they would deny out of distress. The wind that turns vegetation yellow is *ṣirr ḥarur* (a scorching cold wind), and both of these cause the plants to become dry stubble (*hashim*). *Al-ḥarur* is the side of the north wind when it storms. The pronoun in *fa-ra'awhu* refers to what is understood from the context, which is the vegetation. It has been said that it refers to the *athar*, because the mercy is the rain and its trace is the vegetation. As for the one who read *athar* in the plural, he returns the pronoun to the traces of mercy, which is the vegetation. The word for vegetation applies to the few and the many, because it is a verbal noun used as a name for what grows. Ibn ʿIsa said: The pronoun in *fa-ra'awhu* refers to the clouds, because when the clouds turn yellow they do not rain. It has also been said that it refers to the wind, but these two views are weak. Ṣabbah ibn Ḥubaysh read *misfarran*, with an alif after the fa'. The lam in *wa-la-in* signals an oath (qasam) that is omitted, and its answer is *la-zallu* ("they would continue"). This is one of the places where the past tense is used in place of the future for breadth of expression. Its estimate is *la-yazallunna* ("they will certainly continue"). A parallel is His saying: "And even if you brought those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah" [al-Baqarah: 145], meaning "they do not follow." He, may He be exalted, censures them in all their states: they were obligated to rely upon the bounty of Allah, yet they despaired; if they thanked His blessing, they did not go beyond joy and rejoicing; and if they were patient with His trial, they disbelieved. The pronoun in *min baʿdih* ("after it") refers to the yellowing, meaning: after the yellowing of the vegetation you deny His blessing.

The discussion of His saying *fa-innaka la tusmiʿu al-mawta* ("indeed you do not make the dead hear") up to *fa-hum muslimun* ("so they are submitting") has already been given at the end of Surah al-Naml, except that here the connection is made with *fa* in *fa-innaka* ("indeed you").

When he had mentioned the signs of the horizons, he mentioned some of the signs within the self, and he made the creation from weakness (ḍaʿf), because of the great weakness of a human being at the beginning of his life and in his childhood, as in His saying: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya: 37]. The strength that followed weakness is his growth, his flourishing and his vigour until the stage of maturity (al-iktihāl). The weakness that comes after strength is the state of old age and decrepitude. It was said that ﴿from weakness﴾ refers to the drop (of semen), as in His saying: ﴿from a despised fluid﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8]. The alternation of these states is evidence of the power and knowledge of the Creator.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of the reciters) read ḍuʿf with a ḍammah on the ḍād in both places. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it with a fatḥah in both places, and this is the reading of ʿAbdullah and Abu Rajaʾ. It is narrated from Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, al-Jaḥdarī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk: ḍammah and fatḥah on the second. ʿĪsā read it with two ḍammahs in both places. The apparent meaning is that weakness and strength refer to what is other than the body, and that ḍamm and fatḥ have the same meaning in ḍuʿf. Many linguists said: the ḍammah is for the body, and the fatḥah is for the intellect.

(Mā labithū) is an answer (to the question), and it is according to the meaning. For had it reported their words, the construction would have been: mā labithnā ghayra sāʿah (we did not remain but an hour). That is, they did not remain beneath the earth more than an hour. As for their remaining in the world, they considered it little in comparison with what they witnessed of the Hereafter, or (it refers to) the period between the end of the world and the resurrection. Their reporting of this is by way of conjecture and speculation without knowledge, or by way of forgetfulness, or lying. (Yuʾfakūn): that is, they are turned away from speaking the truth and uttering what is true.

﴿Those who were given knowledge﴾ are the angels, the prophets and the believers.

﴿In the Book of God﴾: in what He promised in His Book of the gathering and the resurrection. The knowledge (in the verse) is general and includes faith and other things, but this specific item was mentioned explicitly to honour it and to draw attention to its position within knowledge. It was said: ﴿in the Book of God﴾ means the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was said: in His knowledge; it was said: in His judgment. Al-Ḥasan read al-baʿath with a fatḥah on the ʿayn in both places, and it was also read with a kasrah. The kasrah form is a noun, while the fatḥah form is a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Qatadah said: it is by inversion (al-taqdīm wa al-taʾkhīr), its meaning being: "those who were given knowledge in the Book of God and faith." Al-Zamakhsharī said... (and this is a qualification that stands on its own), and the sense of "in" here is equal to the preposition bāʾ, that is: the knowledge of the Book of God. Perhaps this view is not authentically transmitted from Qatadah, for in it there is a dislocation of the structure which would not be permissible in eloquent speech, so how could it be permissible in the speech of God? Qatadah was described as having knowledge of Arabic, so such a statement would not come from him.

The fāʾ in ﴿fa-hādhā yawmu al-baʿth﴾ (so this is the Day of Resurrection) is conjunctive, linking this spoken sentence to the sentence before it, which is ﴿you have remained﴾; it follows it in the mention. Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you say, what is this fāʾ and what is its real nature? I say: it is the one in the line of the poet:

*Then we have come to Khurasan* (fa-qad jiʾnā Khurāsānā)

Its real nature is that it is the answer to a condition which the speech implies, as if he said: If what you say is true, that the utmost that is intended for us is that we return, then: we have come to Khurasan. And when it is possible to make the fāʾ conjunctive, there is no need to supply a hidden condition, and making the fāʾ an answer to that deleted condition... (the statement continues) "you do not know" because of your neglect in seeking the truth and following it. It was said: "you do not know" the resurrection, and you are not made aware of it, so your destination becomes the Fire, and you seek a postponement.

(Fa-yawmaʾidhin): that is, the Day on which this occurs, namely the swearing of the disbelievers and the words of those with knowledge to them. The Kufans read (lā yanfaʿu) with the yāʾ here and in al-Ṭūl (sura 40), and Nāfiʿ agreed with them in al-Ṭūl; the rest of the seven read it with the feminine tāʾ.

﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends (wa lā hum yustaʿtabūn)﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: from your saying: istaʿtabanī fulān, fa-aʿtabtuhu, that is: he asked me to be pleased and I pleased him, and that is when he (the one wronged) was harmed by him (the wrongdoer). The real meaning is: aʿtabtahu, I removed his grievance. Do you not see his saying:

*Tamīm became angry that ʿĀmir should kill on the day of al-Nisār, so they were made to be pleased at al-Ṣaylam.*

How he made them angry. Then he said: fa-uʿtibū, that is, their anger was removed, and anger has the meaning of grievance. The meaning is: it is not said to them, "Please your Lord with repentance and obedience." Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Today they shall not be brought out from it, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ [al-Jāthiyah: 35]. (If you say): how are they made not asked to make amends in some verses, and not made to make amends in some verses? And His saying: ﴿And if they ask for amends, they will not be of those granted amends﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 24]? I say: as for their not being asked to make amends, this is its meaning; as for their not being made to make amends, its meaning is that they are not content with what they are in. So their state is compared to the state of a people who have been wronged, who are aggrieved at the wrongdoer and not content with him. If they ask God (yastaʿtibū Allāh), that is, ask Him to remove what they are in, they will not be among those who are responded to in its removal.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is a report about the terror of the Day of Resurrection and the severity of its circumstances for the disbelievers, in that their excuse will not benefit them and they will not be given ʿutbā, which is contentment. (Yustaʿtabūn) means the same as (yaʿtibūn), just as you say: yamliku and yustamlaku. The norm for istafʿala is that it seeks something, and this is not that, because the meaning is not spoiled if what is understood from it is: "and they are not asked for ʿutbā." End. So istafʿala here has the meaning of the bare verb ʿataba, that is: they are, in terms of neglect and not being paid attention to, in the position of one who is not qualified to be reproached. It has been said: they are not reproached for their evil deeds, but rather punished. It was said: no one seeks contentment for them. It was said: no work or obedience is required of them. But We have struck (for mankind every kind of parable in this Qur'an) as a sign of removing excuses and bringing forth more than sufficient warning. Al-Zamakhsharī said: We described for them every attribute that is like a parable in its strangeness, and We related to them every story of wondrous matter, such as the description of those raised on the Day of Resurrection, what will be said to them, the excuses that will not be accepted from them, and the requests for contentment that will not be heard from them. But because of the hardness of their hearts and the aversion of their ears to the talk of the Hereafter, when you bring them a sign from the signs of the Qur'an, they say: "Have you brought us falsehood?" End. (Antum) is an address to the Messenger and the believers, that is: you are wrong in your claim of the gathering and the recompense. Abu ʿAbdullah al-Rāzī said: In the unity of address in His saying ﴿And if you (sg.) bring them﴾ and the plural in His saying "Indeed you (pl.)" there is a subtle point, which is: God, mighty and majestic, said ﴿And if you bring them﴾ with every sign that the Messengers brought, so they may answer him with His saying: "You, all of you, O you who claim to be messengers, are wrong."

﴿Thus God seals (yaṭbaʿu)﴾: that is, with such sealing God seals the hearts of the ignorant, those upon whom God has already sealed disbelief from eternity. He attributed the sealing to His own essence, because He is the One who does and decrees it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: The meaning of "God sealed" is that He made the kindnesses by which He opens the breasts so that they accept the truth. Then he said: Thus hearts become corroded and the hearts of the ignorant harden, until they call the people of truth "wrongdoers", while they are the most knowledgeable of God's creation in that attribute. End. This is according to the path of the Muʿtazilah. Then He commanded him, may He be exalted, to be patient with their enmity, and strengthened him by affirming that the promise is true, that it must be fulfilled and carried out, and forbade him from being shaken or moved by their words, for they have no certainty and no insight.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Yaʿqūb read (wa lā yastakhiffannaka), with an unpointed ḥāʾ and a qāf, from al-istiḥqāq (to deserve); the majority read it with a pointed khāʾ and fāʾ, from al-istikhfāf (to make light of). Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Yaʿqūb made the nūn sukūn (unvocalised). The meaning is: "let them not seduce you, and let them not be more entitled to you than the believers."

* *

Sūrat Luqmān is Makkī.

Vocabulary of Sūrat Luqmān

Luqmān: a proper name. If it is non-Arabic, its prohibition from declension is due to foreignness and proper nounhood; if it is Arabic, its prohibition is due to proper nounhood and the addition of the alif and nūn, and it is derived from al-laqm (swallowing), as a proper name (murtajal), since no origin is known for it among indefinite nouns.

Ṣaʿʿara: with a doubled ʿayn, the dialect of Banū Tamīm. Their poet said:

*And we, when the tyrant turned away his cheek, we straightened him from his inclination, so he straightened up.*

Fa-taqawwamā: an imperative for straightness to suit the rhyme in the genitive case, that is: "so let him stand up" if Abu ʿUbaydah said it. The recitation of al-Ṭabarī, "fa-yuqawwamā" as a past verb, is an error. Taṣāʿara is the dialect of the Ḥijāz, and it is said: yuṣaʿʿiru. The poet said:

*We straightened for him from his puffed-up cheek.*

And it is said: aṣʿara khaddahu (he turned his cheek away). Al-Faḍl said: it is inclination. Al-Yazīdī said: it is arrogance in speech. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the origin of this is from ṣaʿar, a disease which affects camels in their heads and necks, so that their necks twist from it.

Al-Qalam: well known (the pen).

Al-Khattār: one who is intensely treacherous. From it is their saying:

*Indeed you do not extend to us a span of treachery, except that we extend to you an arm's length of ... (khatr).*

ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib said:

*And indeed, if you had seen Abu ʿUmayr, you would have filled your hands with treachery and deceit.*

Al-Aʿshā said:

*So the dappled stallion of Taymāʾ, his dwelling is a fortified fortress and a neighbour who is not treacherous.*

When he had mentioned the signs of the horizons, he mentioned some of the signs within the self, and he made the creation from weakness (ḍaʿf), because of the great weakness of a human being at the beginning of his life and in his childhood, as in His saying: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya: 37]. The strength that followed weakness is his growth, his flourishing and his vigour until the stage of maturity (al-iktihāl). The weakness that comes after strength is the state of old age and decrepitude. It was said that ﴿from weakness﴾ refers to the drop (of semen), as in His saying: ﴿from a despised fluid﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8]. The alternation of these states is evidence of the power and knowledge of the Creator.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of the reciters) read ḍuʿf with a ḍammah on the ḍād in both places. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it with a fatḥah in both places, and this is the reading of ʿAbdullah and Abu Rajaʾ. It is narrated from Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, al-Jaḥdarī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk: ḍammah and fatḥah on the second. ʿĪsā read it with two ḍammahs in both places. The apparent meaning is that weakness and strength refer to what is other than the body, and that ḍamm and fatḥ have the same meaning in ḍuʿf. Many linguists said: the ḍammah is for the body, and the fatḥah is for the intellect.

(Mā labithū) is an answer (to the question), and it is according to the meaning. For had it reported their words, the construction would have been: mā labithnā ghayra sāʿah (we did not remain but an hour). That is, they did not remain beneath the earth more than an hour. As for their remaining in the world, they considered it little in comparison with what they witnessed of the Hereafter, or (it refers to) the period between the end of the world and the resurrection. Their reporting of this is by way of conjecture and speculation without knowledge, or by way of forgetfulness, or lying. (Yuʾfakūn): that is, they are turned away from speaking the truth and uttering what is true.

﴿In the Book of God﴾: in what He promised in His Book of the gathering and the resurrection. The knowledge (in the verse) is general and includes faith and other things, but this specific item was mentioned explicitly to honour it and to draw attention to its position within knowledge. It was said: ﴿in the Book of God﴾ means the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was said: in His knowledge; it was said: in His judgment. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends (wa lā hum yustaʿtabūn)﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: from your saying: istaʿtabanī fulān, fa-aʿtabtuhu, that is: he asked me to be pleased and I pleased him, and that is when he (the one wronged) was harmed by him (the wrongdoer). (If you say): how are they made not asked to make amends in some verses, and not made to make amends in some verses? And His saying: ﴿And if they ask for amends, they will not be of those granted amends﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 24]? I say: as for their not being asked to make amends, this is its meaning; as for their not being made to make amends, its meaning is that they are not content with what they are in. So their state is compared to the state of a people who have been wronged, who are aggrieved at the wrongdoer and not content with him. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Today they shall not be brought out from it, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ [al-Jāthiyah: 35]. (If you say): how are they made not asked to make amends in some verses, and not made to make amends in some verses? And His saying: ﴿And if they ask for amends, they will not be of those granted amends﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 24]? I say: as for their not being asked to make amends, this is its meaning; as for their not being made to make amends, its meaning is that they are not content with what they are in. So their state is compared to the state of a people who have been wronged, who are aggrieved at the wrongdoer and not content with him. If they ask God (yastaʿtibū Allāh), that is, ask Him to remove what they are in, they will not be among those who are responded to in its removal.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is a report about the terror of the Day of Resurrection and the severity of its circumstances for the disbelievers, in that their excuse will not benefit them and they will not be given ʿutbā, which is contentment. (Yustaʿtabūn) means the same as (yaʿtibūn), just as you say: yamliku and yustamlaku. The norm for istafʿala is that it seeks something, and this is not that, because the meaning is not spoiled if what is understood from it is: "and they are not asked for ʿutbā." End. So istafʿala here has the meaning of the bare verb ʿataba, that is: they are, in terms of neglect and not being paid attention to, in the position of one who is not qualified to be reproached. It has been said: they are not reproached for their evil deeds, but rather punished. It was said: no one seeks contentment for them. It was said: no work or obedience is required of them. But We have struck (for mankind every kind of parable in this Qur'an) as a sign of removing excuses and bringing forth more than sufficient warning. Al-Zamakhsharī said: We described for them every attribute that is like a parable in its strangeness, and We related to them every story of wondrous matter, such as the description of those raised on the Day of Resurrection, what will be said to them, the excuses that will not be accepted from them, and the requests for contentment that will not be heard from them. But because of the hardness of their hearts and the aversion of their ears to the talk of the Hereafter, when you bring them a sign from the signs of the Qur'an, they say: "Have you brought us falsehood?" End. (Antum) is an address to the Messenger and the believers, that is: you are wrong in your claim of the gathering and the recompense. Abu ʿAbdullah al-Rāzī said: In the unity of address in His saying ﴿And if you (sg.) bring them﴾ and the plural in His saying "Indeed you (pl.)" there is a subtle point, which is: God, mighty and majestic, said ﴿And if you bring them﴾ with every sign that the Messengers brought, so they may answer him with His saying: "You, all of you, O you who claim to be messengers, are wrong."

﴿Thus God seals (yaṭbaʿu)﴾: that is, with such sealing God seals the hearts of the ignorant, those upon whom God has already sealed disbelief from eternity. He attributed the sealing to His own essence, because He is the One who does and decrees it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: The meaning of "God sealed" is that He made the kindnesses by which He opens the breasts so that they accept the truth. Then he said: Thus hearts become corroded and the hearts of the ignorant harden, until they call the people of truth "wrongdoers", while they are the most knowledgeable of God's creation in that attribute. End. This is according to the path of the Muʿtazilah. Then He commanded him, may He be exalted, to be patient with their enmity, and strengthened him by affirming that the promise is true, that it must be fulfilled and carried out, and forbade him from being shaken or moved by their words, for they have no certainty and no insight.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Yaʿqūb read (wa lā yastakhiffannaka), with an unpointed ḥāʾ and a qāf, from al-istiḥqāq (to deserve); the majority read it with a pointed khāʾ and fāʾ, from al-istikhfāf (to make light of). Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Yaʿqūb made the nūn sukūn (unvocalised). The meaning is: "let them not seduce you, and let them not be more entitled to you than the believers."

Sūrat Luqmān is Makkī.

Vocabulary of Sūrat Luqmān

Luqmān: a proper name. If it is non-Arabic, its prohibition from declension is due to foreignness and proper nounhood; if it is Arabic, its prohibition is due to proper nounhood and the addition of the alif and nūn, and it is derived from al-laqm (swallowing), as a proper name (murtajal), since no origin is known for it among indefinite nouns.

Ṣaʿʿara: with a doubled ʿayn, the dialect of Banū Tamīm. Their poet said:

*And we, when the tyrant turned away his cheek, we straightened him from his inclination, so he straightened up.*

Fa-taqawwamā: an imperative for straightness to suit the rhyme in the genitive case, that is: "so let him stand up" if Abu ʿUbaydah said it. The recitation of al-Ṭabarī, "fa-yuqawwamā" as a past verb, is an error. Taṣāʿara is the dialect of the Ḥijāz, and it is said: yuṣaʿʿiru. The poet said:

*We straightened for him from his puffed-up cheek.*

And it is said: aṣʿara khaddahu (he turned his cheek away). Al-Faḍl said: it is inclination. Al-Yazīdī said: it is arrogance in speech. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the origin of this is from ṣaʿar, a disease which affects camels in their heads and necks, so that their necks twist from it.

Al-Qalam: well known (the pen).

Al-Khattār: one who is intensely treacherous. From it is their saying:

*Indeed you do not extend to us a span of treachery, except that we extend to you an arm's length of ... (khatr).*

ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib said:

*And indeed, if you had seen Abu ʿUmayr, you would have filled your hands with treachery and deceit.*

Al-Aʿshā said:

*So the dappled stallion of Taymāʾ, his dwelling is a fortified fortress and a neighbour who is not treacherous.*
